q: Charles Babbage designed a machine with a 'mill' (to do the calculations) and a 'store' (to hold numbers). What was this machine called?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The Analytical Engine (designed from 1837) had a mill, like today's CPU, and a store, like today's memory.
concept: Charles Babbage is called the father of the computer. His first design, the Difference Engine (1822), could only work out tables of numbers. His later Analytical Engine (1837) was a general-purpose design with a mill (processing unit), a store (memory) and punched-card input, so it had the main parts of a modern computer.
why: A — Wrong. The Difference Engine (1822) was Babbage's earlier machine for calculating mathematical tables; it had no separate mill and store.
B — Correct. The Analytical Engine had a mill that did the arithmetic and a store that held numbers, the ideas behind today's CPU and memory.
C — Wrong. The Stepped Reckoner was a mechanical calculator built by Gottfried Leibniz in the 17th century, not by Babbage.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Mill = CPU, Store = memory: remember this pairing for the Analytical Engine.

q: Who is regarded as the first computer programmer because of the notes she wrote in 1843 on Babbage's Analytical Engine?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Ada Lovelace's 1843 notes contain a step-by-step method for the Analytical Engine to compute Bernoulli numbers, which is called the first computer program.
concept: Ada Lovelace translated an article about the Analytical Engine and added long notes of her own. One note gave step-by-step instructions for the machine to calculate Bernoulli numbers. Because of this she is widely called the first computer programmer. The programming language Ada is named after her.
why: A — Correct. Ada Lovelace's 1843 notes contain an algorithm written for the Analytical Engine, so she is called the first programmer.
B — Wrong. Grace Hopper worked in the 20th century; she built early compilers and helped shape COBOL, but she is not called the first programmer.
C — Wrong. Hedy Lamarr was an actress who co-invented a frequency-hopping radio idea; she wrote no programs for Babbage's engine.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The Pascaline (1642), a mechanical calculator made by Blaise Pascal, was designed mainly to perform:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The Pascaline was a gear-driven adding machine; it added and subtracted directly.
concept: Blaise Pascal built the Pascaline in 1642 to help his father, a tax official, with long additions. It used toothed wheels: when one wheel passed 9 it moved the next wheel on by one (a carry). It could add and subtract directly; multiplication and division needed repeated additions or subtractions by the user.
why: A — Wrong. The Pascaline could not multiply or divide directly (only by repeating additions or subtractions), so 'multiplication and division only' is false.
B — Wrong. Logical operations such as AND and OR belong to modern digital circuits, not to a 17th-century gear calculator.
C — Correct. Addition and subtraction were the Pascaline's main operations.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Who built the Stepped Reckoner, a 17th-century mechanical calculator that could also multiply and divide?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The Stepped Reckoner was built by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, who is not among options A–C.
concept: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, a German mathematician, built the Stepped Reckoner (first shown in 1673). Its stepped drum, called the Leibniz wheel, let it multiply and divide by repeated addition and subtraction done by the machine. Leibniz also wrote about the binary number system that modern computers use.
why: A — Wrong. Blaise Pascal built the Pascaline (1642), an adding and subtracting machine, not the Stepped Reckoner.
B — Wrong. John Napier invented logarithms and Napier's Bones (1617), a set of numbered rods that help with multiplication.
C — Wrong. Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine and the Analytical Engine in the 19th century.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. The Stepped Reckoner was built by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, who is not listed in A–C.
tip: Pascal = Pascaline (add/subtract); Leibniz = Stepped Reckoner (could also multiply/divide).

q: The loom of 1804 that used punched cards to control the pattern of woven cloth was invented by:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Joseph Marie Jacquard's loom (1804) read a chain of punched cards to decide the weaving pattern.
concept: In the Jacquard loom each punched card stood for one row of the pattern: a hole let a thread hook rise and a blank stopped it. This showed that a machine could be controlled by instructions stored on cards. Babbage planned to use similar cards for the Analytical Engine, and Hollerith later used punched cards to store data.
why: A — Correct. Joseph Marie Jacquard built the punched-card loom in 1804.
B — Wrong. Herman Hollerith used punched cards for data processing in the 1890 US census, more than 80 years after Jacquard's loom.
C — Wrong. Howard Aiken designed the Harvard Mark I computer (1944), not a loom.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: An inventor built a punched-card tabulating machine that processed the 1890 US census. His company later became part of which well-known company?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The inventor is Herman Hollerith; his Tabulating Machine Company merged into CTR in 1911, which was renamed IBM in 1924.
concept: Step 1: the punched-card tabulator used for the 1890 US census was made by Herman Hollerith. Step 2: Hollerith founded the Tabulating Machine Company in 1896. In 1911 it merged with other firms to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company (CTR), which took the name International Business Machines (IBM) in 1924.
why: A — Wrong. Microsoft was founded in 1975 by Bill Gates and Paul Allen; it has no link with Hollerith's company.
B — Correct. Hollerith's company became part of CTR, which was renamed IBM in 1924.
C — Wrong. Intel was founded in 1968 by Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore; it made microchips, not punched-card tabulators.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Hollerith → Tabulating Machine Company (1896) → CTR (1911) → IBM (1924).

q: Which of the following device–inventor pairs are correctly matched?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three pairs are correct, so more than one option is true.
concept: Early calculating aids: Napier's Bones (1617, John Napier) were numbered rods that made multiplication easier; the slide rule (about 1622, William Oughtred) used logarithmic scales; the Pascaline (1642, Blaise Pascal) was a geared adding machine. All of these came long before electronic computers.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. John Napier made Napier's Bones in 1617 to make multiplication easier.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. William Oughtred made the slide rule (about 1622) using Napier's logarithms.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Blaise Pascal made the Pascaline in 1642.
D — Correct. All three pairs in A, B and C are correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Some books also mention Edmund Gunter, who made a single logarithmic scale (Gunter's scale) in 1620; the slide rule with two scales sliding against each other is credited to William Oughtred (about 1622).

q: In 1936, who described an abstract 'universal machine' that became the theoretical model of every modern computer?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Alan Turing's 1936 paper described the Turing machine, a simple abstract model of computation.
concept: A Turing machine reads and writes symbols on an endless tape, following a table of rules. Turing showed that one 'universal' machine could imitate any other such machine if it is given that machine's rules as data. This idea is the basis of general-purpose computers. Turing also proposed the Turing test (1950) for machine intelligence, and the Turing Award, the top prize in computing, is named after him.
why: A — Correct. Alan Turing described the universal (Turing) machine in 1936.
B — Wrong. John von Neumann is known for the stored-program design of 1945 (von Neumann architecture), not for the 1936 universal machine paper.
C — Wrong. Charles Babbage died in 1871; he designed mechanical engines, not the 1936 abstract machine.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The 'stored-program concept', in which program instructions are kept in memory along with the data, is mainly credited to:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: John von Neumann described the stored-program design in his 1945 report on the EDVAC.
concept: In 1945 John von Neumann wrote the 'First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC'. It described a computer with an arithmetic unit, a control unit, memory, input and output, in which the program is stored in the same memory as the data. Computers built this way follow the von Neumann architecture, and most computers today still do.
why: A — Wrong. Babbage's Analytical Engine was to read its instructions from punched cards; it did not keep its program in its store (memory).
B — Correct. The stored-program concept is credited to John von Neumann (1945).
C — Wrong. Herman Hollerith built punched-card tabulating machines for counting census data; they were not stored-program computers.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Books note that Eckert and Mauchly also worked on the idea, but exams credit the stored-program concept to von Neumann.

q: ENIAC, shown to the public in 1946 at the University of Pennsylvania, was built by:
opts: J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly
More than one of the above
exp: ENIAC was designed and built by J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly.
concept: ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was built for the US Army to calculate artillery firing tables. It used about 18,000 vacuum tubes, weighed about 30 tons and filled a large room. It is generally called the first general-purpose electronic digital computer. It was programmed by setting switches and plugging cables.
why: A — Wrong. Howard Aiken and IBM built the Harvard Mark I (1944), an electromechanical computer.
B — Wrong. Maurice Wilkes led the EDSAC project at Cambridge University, England (1949).
C — Correct. J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly designed and built ENIAC.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: ENIAC = Eckert & Mauchly; EDSAC = Maurice Wilkes; Harvard Mark I = Howard Aiken; UNIVAC I = first commercial computer in the USA.

q:
Consider the following statements about ENIAC:
I. It used vacuum tubes as its switching elements.
II. It was built at the University of Pennsylvania.
III. It was designed by Charles Babbage.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because ENIAC was designed by Eckert and Mauchly in the 1940s, long after Babbage died (1871).
concept: ENIAC was built at the Moore School of Electrical Engineering, University of Pennsylvania, by J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, and was shown to the public in 1946. It used about 18,000 vacuum tubes, which makes it a first-generation computer.
why: A — Correct. Statements I and II are true and III is false.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: Babbage died in 1871, and ENIAC was designed by Eckert and Mauchly.
C — Wrong. III is false, so all three statements cannot be correct.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which computer, delivered to the US Census Bureau in 1951, is known as the first commercial computer produced in the USA?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: UNIVAC I, built by the company of Eckert and Mauchly, was delivered to the US Census Bureau in 1951.
concept: UNIVAC stands for UNIVersal Automatic Computer. UNIVAC I was a first-generation (vacuum-tube) computer that used magnetic tape for input and output. It became famous when it correctly predicted the result of the 1952 US presidential election. Britain also had early commercial machines (Ferranti Mark 1, LEO I), so the exam phrase is 'first commercial computer in the USA'.
why: A — Wrong. ENIAC was built for the US Army as a one-off machine; it was never sold commercially.
B — Correct. UNIVAC I (1951) was the first commercial computer produced in the USA.
C — Wrong. EDSAC was built at Cambridge University in England (1949) for research, not as a US commercial product.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The Harvard Mark I (1944), an electromechanical computer also called the IBM ASCC, was designed by:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Howard Aiken of Harvard University designed the Mark I, and IBM built it.
concept: The Harvard Mark I (IBM Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator) used relays, switches and rotating shafts, so it was electromechanical rather than fully electronic. It read its instructions from punched paper tape. Aiken was inspired by Babbage's Analytical Engine. The term 'Harvard architecture' (separate storage for instructions and data) comes from this machine.
why: A — Wrong. Babbage died in 1871; he designed mechanical engines, not the Mark I.
B — Wrong. John Mauchly co-designed ENIAC with Eckert; ENIAC was fully electronic.
C — Correct. Howard Aiken designed the Harvard Mark I.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The transistor was invented in 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley at:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: They worked at Bell Telephone Laboratories (Bell Labs), which is not among options A–C.
concept: The transistor is a small semiconductor device that can switch and amplify electric signals. It was invented at Bell Labs in 1947, and its three inventors shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. Transistors replaced vacuum tubes in second-generation computers, making them smaller, faster, cheaper and cooler.
why: A — Wrong. IBM later built transistor computers, but the transistor was not invented there.
B — Wrong. Intel was founded in 1968, about 20 years after the transistor was invented.
C — Wrong. Texas Instruments is famous for Jack Kilby's integrated circuit (1958), not for inventing the transistor.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. The transistor was invented at Bell Labs, which is not listed in A–C.
tip: Transistor = Bell Labs (1947); IC = Kilby at Texas Instruments and Noyce at Fairchild (1958–59).

q: The integrated circuit (IC) was invented independently in 1958–59 by which of the following?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce invented the IC independently; Shockley co-invented the transistor.
concept: Jack Kilby of Texas Instruments made the first working IC in 1958 and later received the Nobel Prize in Physics (2000). Robert Noyce of Fairchild Semiconductor made a practical silicon IC in 1959 and later co-founded Intel. An IC places many transistors and other parts on one small chip of semiconductor, usually silicon. ICs are the basis of third-generation computers.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Jack Kilby built the first working IC at Texas Instruments in 1958.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Robert Noyce independently made a silicon IC at Fairchild Semiconductor in 1959.
C — Wrong. William Shockley was a co-inventor of the transistor (1947), not of the integrated circuit.
D — Correct. Both A and B are true, so more than one of the above is correct.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Intel's first microprocessor, released in 1971, was the:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The Intel 4004 (1971) was Intel's first microprocessor, a 4-bit CPU on a single chip.
concept: A microprocessor puts the whole CPU on one chip. The Intel 4004 (1971) was a 4-bit microprocessor designed by a team that included Ted Hoff, Federico Faggin and Stanley Mazor. Microprocessors began the fourth generation of computers and made personal computers possible.
why: A — Correct. The Intel 4004 was released in 1971.
B — Wrong. The 8085 is a later 8-bit microprocessor (1976) with a 16-bit address bus.
C — Wrong. The 8086 is a 16-bit microprocessor released in 1978; the IBM PC used its close relative, the 8088.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Who invented the computer mouse in the 1960s and showed it publicly in 1968?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Douglas Engelbart invented the mouse and demonstrated it in his famous 1968 demonstration.
concept: Douglas Engelbart and his team at the Stanford Research Institute built the first mouse: a wooden box with two wheels underneath. Engelbart showed it in 1968 in a demonstration that also showed windows, hypertext and video conferencing. The mouse became popular with the Apple Macintosh (1984).
why: A — Wrong. Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN (proposal in 1989).
B — Correct. Douglas Engelbart invented the computer mouse.
C — Wrong. Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email in 1971 and chose the @ sign.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
opts: Ray Tomlinson — first network email using the @ sign
More than one of the above
exp: Vint Cerf co-designed TCP/IP; the Intel 4004 was designed at Intel by Ted Hoff, Federico Faggin and others.
concept: Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers on ARPANET in 1971 and used @ to separate the user name from the computer name. Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989. Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn designed TCP/IP, the basic protocols of the Internet, so they are called the fathers of the Internet.
why: A — Wrong. This pair is correct, so it does not satisfy the NOT stem: Tomlinson sent the first network email in 1971 and used @.
B — Wrong. This pair is correct: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN.
C — Correct. This pair is wrong: Vint Cerf is known for TCP/IP, not for the Intel 4004.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q:
Consider the following statements about computing in India:
I. HEC-2M, installed at the Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata, in 1956, was the first computer installed in India.
II. PARAM 8000 was developed by C-DAC.
III. PARAM 8000 was the first computer designed and built in India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because TIFRAC (about 1960) was the first computer designed and built in India, three decades before PARAM 8000 (1991).
concept: HEC-2M (Hollerith Electronic Computer) came from Britain and was installed at ISI Kolkata in 1956, the first computer in India. TIFRAC, built at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), Mumbai, and working by 1960, was the first computer designed and built in India. PARAM 8000 (1991), built by C-DAC, Pune, was India's first supercomputer.
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is also true, so 'I only' leaves out a correct statement.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: the first computer designed and built in India was TIFRAC (about 1960).
C — Correct. Statements I and II are true and III is false.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: First computer installed in India = HEC-2M (ISI Kolkata, 1956); first designed in India = TIFRAC (TIFR, 1960); first Indian supercomputer = PARAM 8000 (C-DAC, 1991).

q: TIFRAC, the first computer designed and built in India, was developed at:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: TIFRAC was developed at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), Mumbai, which is not among A–C.
concept: TIFRAC stands for Tata Institute of Fundamental Research Automatic Calculator. It was designed and built by Indian scientists at TIFR, Mumbai (then Bombay), and was working by 1960. It was a first-generation machine using vacuum tubes and ferrite-core memory.
why: A — Wrong. ISI Kolkata installed HEC-2M (1956), a computer brought from Britain; it did not build TIFRAC.
B — Wrong. C-DAC was set up in 1988 and built the PARAM supercomputers, long after TIFRAC.
C — Wrong. IIT Kanpur is known for early computer education in India, but TIFRAC was not built there.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. TIFRAC was built at TIFR, Mumbai, which is not listed in A–C.

q: Public (commercial) Internet service in India was launched on 15 August 1995 by:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Videsh Sanchar Nigam Limited (VSNL) launched public Internet access in India on 15 August 1995.
concept: VSNL, then the government's international telecom company, opened Internet access to the public on 15 August 1995 using dial-up connections. Before that, ERNET (Education and Research Network, started in 1986) connected only academic and research institutions. BSNL was formed later, in 2000.
why: A — Correct. VSNL launched public Internet service on 15 August 1995.
B — Wrong. BSNL (Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited) was formed in 2000, five years after this launch.
C — Wrong. ERNET (1986) linked universities and research centres; it was not the public service launched in 1995.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Public Internet in India = VSNL, 15 August 1995; academic network ERNET started earlier, in 1986.

q:
Arrange the following in chronological order (earliest first):
1. ENIAC shown to the public
2. Intel 4004 released
3. Transistor invented
4. Analytical Engine designed

exp: Analytical Engine (1837) → ENIAC (1946) → transistor (1947) → Intel 4004 (1971), so the order is 4, 1, 3, 2.
concept: Timeline: Analytical Engine designed (1837) → ENIAC shown to the public (February 1946) → transistor invented at Bell Labs (December 1947) → Intel 4004 microprocessor (1971). ENIAC used vacuum tubes because the transistor did not yet exist.
why: A — Wrong. It puts the transistor (1947) before ENIAC (1946); ENIAC came first, which is why it used vacuum tubes.
C — Wrong. It puts ENIAC (1946) before the Analytical Engine (1837), which was designed more than a century earlier.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.

q: The main electronic component used for switching and processing in first-generation computers was the:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: First-generation computers were built with vacuum tubes (also called valves).
concept: First-generation computers (roughly the 1940s to the mid-1950s) used vacuum tubes. Tubes were large, used much power, produced a lot of heat and failed often, so these computers were huge, costly and unreliable. They were programmed mainly in machine language and used punched cards and paper tape for input and output.
why: A — Correct. The vacuum tube was the main component of the first generation.
B — Wrong. Transistors were the main component of the second generation.
C — Wrong. Integrated circuits were the main component of the third generation.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Computers such as the IBM 1401 and the IBM 7094 belong to which generation?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The IBM 1401 and IBM 7094 were transistor computers, so they belong to the second generation.
concept: The IBM 1401 (1959) and the IBM 7090 (1959) and IBM 7094 (1962) were built with transistors. Other features of the second generation were magnetic core main memory, magnetic tape and disk storage, and programming in assembly language and early high-level languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL.
why: A — Wrong. First-generation computers used vacuum tubes; examples are ENIAC, EDVAC, UNIVAC I and IBM 701.
B — Correct. The IBM 1401 and IBM 7094 are second-generation (transistor) computers.
C — Wrong. Third-generation computers used integrated circuits; the IBM System/360 is the usual example.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The IBM System/360 (1964) is a well-known example of which generation of computers?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Textbooks give the IBM System/360 as the standard example of a third-generation (integrated circuit) computer.
concept: Third-generation computers (about 1964–1971) used integrated circuits. The IBM System/360 family is the usual textbook example; the PDP-11 is another. These machines were smaller and more reliable, used keyboards and monitors, and ran operating systems that supported multiprogramming and time-sharing.
why: A — Wrong. First-generation computers (such as ENIAC and UNIVAC I) used vacuum tubes and came long before 1964.
B — Wrong. Second-generation computers used discrete transistors; the IBM 1401 is an example.
C — Correct. The IBM System/360 is a third-generation computer.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A computer used vacuum tubes, was programmed in machine language, and used punched cards and a magnetic drum. Which generation did it belong to?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Vacuum tubes and machine-language programming mark the first generation, which is not among A–C.
concept: The switching component decides the generation: vacuum tubes = first, transistors = second, integrated circuits = third, VLSI microprocessors = fourth. First-generation machines were programmed in machine language, used punched cards and paper tape for input and output, and often used magnetic drums for memory.
why: A — Wrong. Second-generation computers used transistors, not vacuum tubes.
B — Wrong. Third-generation computers used integrated circuits.
C — Wrong. Fourth-generation computers used VLSI microprocessors.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. These are first-generation features, and the first generation is not listed in A–C.

q: Which of the following were features of second-generation computers?
opts: Transistors as the main switching component
Magnetic core memory as main memory
Assembly language and early high-level languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL
More than one of the above
exp: All three are second-generation features, so more than one option is true.
concept: Second-generation computers (about 1956–1963) used transistors, which were smaller, faster, cooler and more reliable than vacuum tubes. Main memory was magnetic core memory, and magnetic tape and disks gave secondary storage. Programmers used assembly language and also the first high-level languages, FORTRAN (1957) and COBOL (1959).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Transistors replaced vacuum tubes in the second generation.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Magnetic core memory was the main memory of second-generation machines.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Assembly language and the first high-level languages, FORTRAN (1957) and COBOL (1959), were used in this generation.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of the above is correct.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: some notes say high-level languages began only in the third generation. FORTRAN (1957) and COBOL (1959) were already used in the second generation.

q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of fourth-generation computers?
opts: Vacuum tubes as the main component
More than one of the above
exp: Vacuum tubes belong to the first generation, not the fourth.
concept: The fourth generation (from 1971) is based on the microprocessor, made with VLSI (very large scale integration), which puts thousands to millions of transistors on one chip. Main memory became semiconductor RAM and ROM. Personal computers such as the IBM PC and the Apple II belong to this generation.
why: A — Correct. Vacuum tubes are a first-generation feature, so this is NOT a fourth-generation feature.
B — Wrong. VLSI microprocessors are the defining feature of the fourth generation, so this does not satisfy the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. Semiconductor memory (RAM and ROM) replaced magnetic core memory in this generation, so it is a true feature.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which goal is most closely linked with fifth-generation computers?
opts: Artificial intelligence and understanding natural language
More than one of the above
exp: Fifth-generation computers aim at artificial intelligence, such as understanding natural (human) language.
concept: Fifth-generation computers (present and beyond) aim at artificial intelligence (AI): understanding human language, learning, reasoning, and recognising speech and images. They use ULSI chips and parallel processing. Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Systems project (1982) made the term popular.
why: A — Wrong. Batch processing with punched cards is typical of the first and second generations.
B — Wrong. Magnetic drum memory was used in first-generation computers.
C — Correct. AI and natural-language understanding are the main goals of the fifth generation.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Third-generation computers used integrated circuits.
II. Fourth-generation computers are based on microprocessors made with VLSI.
III. First-generation computers used transistors.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because first-generation computers used vacuum tubes.
concept: Generation and main component: first — vacuum tubes; second — transistors; third — integrated circuits; fourth — VLSI microprocessors; fifth — ULSI and artificial intelligence. Exact years differ between books, but this order of technologies does not.
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is also true, so 'I only' is incomplete.
B — Correct. I and II are true; III is false because transistors came in the second generation.
C — Wrong. III is false, so all three statements cannot be correct.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Generation years differ from book to book; learn the technology of each generation, which every book agrees on.

q: Which of the following generation–technology pairs is NOT correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three pairs are correct, so none of A–C is an incorrect pair.
concept: The main switching technology of each generation is: first — vacuum tubes; second — transistors; third — integrated circuits (ICs); fourth — VLSI microprocessors; fifth — ULSI chips with artificial intelligence.
why: A — Wrong. This pair is correct, so it does not satisfy the NOT stem: the first generation used vacuum tubes.
B — Wrong. This pair is correct: the second generation used transistors.
C — Wrong. This pair is correct: the third generation used integrated circuits.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. All three pairs are correct, so none of them is 'NOT correct'.

q: Moving from first-generation to fourth-generation computers, which change took place?
opts: Computers needed more electricity for the same work
Computers became smaller and produced less heat
More than one of the above
exp: Each new generation used smaller switching parts, so computers became smaller, cooler, faster and more reliable.
concept: Each generation replaced the main switching part with a smaller one: vacuum tube → transistor → integrated circuit → VLSI microprocessor. As a result computers became smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable, and they used less power and produced less heat.
why: A — Wrong. Power use for the same work fell sharply; vacuum tubes used far more electricity than microchips.
B — Wrong. Reliability improved: vacuum tubes burned out often, while transistors and chips rarely fail.
C — Correct. Computers became smaller and produced less heat with each generation.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT a first-generation computer?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The IBM PC (1981) used a microprocessor, so it is a fourth-generation computer.
concept: First-generation (vacuum-tube) computers include ENIAC, EDVAC, EDSAC, UNIVAC I, IBM 650 and IBM 701. The IBM PC (1981) used the Intel 8088 microprocessor, which makes it a fourth-generation computer.
why: A — Wrong. ENIAC used vacuum tubes, so it is a first-generation computer and does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. UNIVAC I (1951) used vacuum tubes, so it is a first-generation computer.
C — Correct. The IBM PC is a fourth-generation (microprocessor) computer, so it is NOT first generation.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q:
Arrange the main switching technologies in the order of computer generations (earliest first):
1. Integrated circuits
2. Vacuum tubes
3. VLSI microprocessors
4. Transistors
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Vacuum tubes → transistors → integrated circuits → VLSI microprocessors, which is 2, 4, 1, 3.
concept: First generation: vacuum tubes. Second: transistors. Third: integrated circuits. Fourth: VLSI microprocessors. Each step packed the same switching job into a smaller, cheaper and more reliable part.
why: A — Wrong. It puts integrated circuits (third generation) before transistors (second generation).
B — Wrong. It puts transistors before vacuum tubes; vacuum tubes came first.
C — Correct. 2 (vacuum tubes), 4 (transistors), 1 (ICs), 3 (VLSI microprocessors).
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: FORTRAN (1957), one of the first widely used high-level languages, was developed at IBM by a team led by:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: John Backus led the IBM team that created FORTRAN.
concept: FORTRAN stands for FORmula TRANslation. It was designed for scientific and engineering calculations. John Backus led the IBM team that released it in 1957. Backus is also known for the Backus–Naur Form (BNF), a notation used to describe the grammar of programming languages.
why: A — Wrong. Dennis Ritchie created the C language (about 1972) at Bell Labs.
B — Correct. John Backus led the FORTRAN team at IBM.
C — Wrong. Niklaus Wirth designed Pascal (1970).
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: LISP (1958), a language long used in artificial intelligence research, was created by:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: John McCarthy created LISP in 1958.
concept: LISP (LISt Processing) was created by John McCarthy in 1958. It is the second-oldest high-level language still in common use, after FORTRAN, and was the main language of early AI research. McCarthy also coined the term 'artificial intelligence' for the 1956 Dartmouth conference.
why: A — Correct. John McCarthy created LISP.
B — Wrong. Guido van Rossum created Python (first released in 1991).
C — Wrong. James Gosling created Java (1995) at Sun Microsystems.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: LISP → artificial intelligence; McCarthy also coined the term 'artificial intelligence'.

q: BASIC was developed in 1964 at Dartmouth College by:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: BASIC was created by John G. Kemeny and Thomas E. Kurtz, who are not among A–C.
concept: BASIC (Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code) was created in 1964 by John G. Kemeny and Thomas E. Kurtz at Dartmouth College, USA, so that students who were not science specialists could write programs easily. Microsoft's first product (1975) was a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800 computer.
why: A — Wrong. Bjarne Stroustrup created C++ (1983) at Bell Labs.
B — Wrong. Brendan Eich created JavaScript (1995) at Netscape.
C — Wrong. Linus Torvalds wrote the Linux kernel (1991).
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. BASIC was created by Kemeny and Kurtz, who are not listed in A–C.

q: The programming language Pascal (1970) was designed by:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Niklaus Wirth designed Pascal and named it after Blaise Pascal.
concept: Niklaus Wirth, a Swiss computer scientist, designed Pascal in 1970 to teach structured programming. He named it after the French mathematician Blaise Pascal, who built the Pascaline. Wirth later designed Modula-2 and Oberon.
why: A — Wrong. Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) built the Pascaline; the language is only named after him.
B — Wrong. Dennis Ritchie created the C language at Bell Labs.
C — Correct. Niklaus Wirth designed Pascal.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Pascal the language is NAMED after Blaise Pascal but DESIGNED by Niklaus Wirth.

q: Which of the following were created at Bell Labs (AT&T)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: C, Unix and C++ were all created at Bell Labs, so more than one option is true.
concept: At Bell Labs, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie developed Unix (from 1969). Ritchie created C (about 1972), and Unix was rewritten in C in 1973, which made it easy to move to other computers. Bjarne Stroustrup created C++ at Bell Labs; it began as 'C with Classes' in 1979 and was named C++ in 1983.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Dennis Ritchie created C at Bell Labs.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie developed Unix at Bell Labs.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Bjarne Stroustrup created C++ at Bell Labs.
D — Correct. A, B and C were all created at Bell Labs, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Java was created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems; Brendan Eich created JavaScript.
concept: Python was created by Guido van Rossum (first released 1991). Java was created by James Gosling and his team at Sun Microsystems (released 1995). Brendan Eich created JavaScript at Netscape in 1995; it is a different language despite the similar name. MS-DOS was released by Microsoft in 1981 for the IBM PC, and Windows 1.0 followed in 1985.
why: A — Wrong. This pair is correct, so it does not satisfy the NOT stem: Guido van Rossum created Python.
B — Correct. This pair is wrong: Java was created by James Gosling; Brendan Eich created JavaScript.
C — Wrong. This pair is correct: Microsoft released MS-DOS in 1981.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Java ≠ JavaScript: Java = James Gosling (Sun); JavaScript = Brendan Eich (Netscape).

q: The Linux kernel was first written in 1991 by:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Linus Torvalds, a Finnish student, released the first Linux kernel in 1991.
concept: Linus Torvalds released the first Linux kernel in 1991 as a free Unix-like kernel. Together with the GNU tools (the GNU Project was started by Richard Stallman in 1983), it forms Linux operating systems such as Ubuntu and Fedora. Linux is open source under the GNU GPL licence, and Android also uses the Linux kernel.
why: A — Correct. Linus Torvalds wrote the Linux kernel.
B — Wrong. Richard Stallman started the GNU Project (1983) and the Free Software Foundation (1985); he did not write the Linux kernel.
C — Wrong. Ken Thompson co-created Unix (1969) at Bell Labs, not Linux.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q:
Arrange the following languages in the order of their first release (earliest first):
1. Java
2. C
3. FORTRAN
4. Python
opts: More than one of the above
exp: FORTRAN (1957) → C (1972) → Python (1991) → Java (1995), which is 3, 2, 4, 1.
concept: Release years: FORTRAN 1957 (John Backus), C about 1972 (Dennis Ritchie), Python 1991 (Guido van Rossum), Java 1995 (James Gosling). Python is older than Java, which surprises many students.
why: A — Wrong. It puts Java (1995) before Python (1991).
B — Wrong. It puts C (1972) before FORTRAN (1957).
C — Correct. 3 (FORTRAN), 2 (C), 4 (Python), 1 (Java).
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A computer that works on continuously varying physical quantities such as voltage, pressure or temperature is called a/an:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: An analog computer measures continuously varying quantities.
concept: By the type of data they handle, computers are analog, digital or hybrid. An analog computer measures continuously varying quantities (voltage, temperature, speed, pressure). A digital computer counts discrete values, usually binary 0 and 1. A hybrid computer combines both. Examples of analog devices: a needle speedometer, a mercury thermometer, a slide rule.
why: A — Correct. Analog computers work on continuous quantities.
B — Wrong. A digital computer works on discrete values (digits, usually 0 and 1); it counts rather than measures.
C — Wrong. 'Microcomputer' is a size class (a personal computer); it is built around a digital microprocessor.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A computer that combines the features of analog and digital computers is called a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A hybrid computer combines analog and digital parts.
concept: A hybrid computer has analog parts that measure continuous signals quickly and digital parts that calculate precisely and control the system. Examples given in books include patient-monitoring systems in hospital ICUs and some industrial process-control systems.
why: A — Wrong. 'Mainframe' is a size class (a large multi-user computer), not a mix of analog and digital.
B — Wrong. 'Minicomputer' is a size class (a mid-range computer), not a mix of analog and digital.
C — Correct. A hybrid computer combines analog and digital features.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Analog measures, digital counts, hybrid does both.

q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of a mainframe computer?
opts: It supports hundreds or thousands of users at the same time
It is designed to be used by only one person at a time
It processes very large numbers of transactions, as in banks and airline reservations
More than one of the above
exp: Mainframes are multi-user systems; a one-person computer is a microcomputer or workstation.
concept: Mainframes are large, powerful and very reliable computers used by big organisations such as banks, insurance companies, railways and airlines. They serve many users and terminals at once and handle huge volumes of transactions (bulk data processing). IBM's Z series is a well-known mainframe family.
why: A — Wrong. Serving many users at once is a true mainframe feature, so it does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Correct. A mainframe is NOT a single-user machine; single-user computers are microcomputers or workstations.
C — Wrong. Bulk transaction processing (banking, reservations) is the classic mainframe job.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The DEC PDP-8, released in 1965, is a famous example of which type of computer?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The PDP-8 was a minicomputer, which is not among A–C.
concept: A minicomputer (mid-range computer) is smaller and cheaper than a mainframe but more powerful than a microcomputer, and it can serve several users at once. Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) made the best-known ones: the PDP-8 (1965), often called the first commercially successful minicomputer, and later the PDP-11.
why: A — Wrong. Supercomputers are the fastest machines (for example the CDC 6600 and CRAY-1); the PDP-8 was a small, low-cost machine.
B — Wrong. Mainframes are large, very costly systems for big organisations; the PDP-8 was designed to be much smaller and cheaper.
C — Wrong. A microcomputer is built around a single-chip microprocessor, and microprocessors appeared only in 1971, after the PDP-8.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. The PDP-8 was a minicomputer, which is not listed in A–C.
tip: Common mistake: some notes write 'miniframe'. The correct term is minicomputer.

q: Which of the following is NOT a microcomputer?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The CRAY-1 (1976) was a supercomputer, not a microcomputer.
concept: A microcomputer is a computer whose CPU is a microprocessor and which is meant mainly for one user. Desktops, laptops, notebooks, tablets and smartphones are all microcomputers (personal computers). The CRAY-1 (1976), designed by Seymour Cray, was a supercomputer.
why: A — Correct. The CRAY-1 is a supercomputer, so it is NOT a microcomputer.
B — Wrong. A laptop is a portable personal computer built around a microprocessor, so it is a microcomputer.
C — Wrong. A tablet is also a microprocessor-based personal device, so it is a microcomputer.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A powerful single-user computer used for CAD, 3-D graphics, animation and scientific design work is called a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A workstation is a high-performance computer for one user doing technical or graphics work.
concept: A workstation is a high-end computer meant for one user doing technical work. It has a fast CPU, more memory, a powerful graphics card and a high-resolution display. Engineers, architects, animators and video editors use workstations. Mainframes and supercomputers are very large shared systems.
why: A — Wrong. A mainframe serves many users at once, mainly for business transactions.
B — Wrong. A supercomputer is a huge shared system for enormous scientific calculations such as weather forecasting.
C — Correct. A workstation is a powerful single-user computer for CAD and graphics.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: a games console such as a PlayStation is not a workstation.

q: Which of the following are examples of embedded systems?
opts: The microcontroller that controls a washing machine
The control chip inside a microwave oven
The anti-lock braking (ABS) controller in a car
More than one of the above
exp: All three are special-purpose computers built into larger devices, so more than one option is true.
concept: An embedded system is a special-purpose computer built into a larger device to control it. It usually has a microcontroller (CPU, memory and input/output on one chip) running fixed firmware. Examples: washing machines, microwave ovens, ABS and engine controllers in cars, digital cameras, smart TVs and traffic-light controllers.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A washing machine's microcontroller is a computer built into the machine to control it.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A microwave oven's control chip runs fixed firmware for timing and power.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The ABS controller is an embedded computer that controls the brakes.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all embedded systems, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. A general-purpose computer can run many different kinds of programs.
II. A special-purpose computer is designed to perform one particular task.
III. A traffic-light controller is an example of a general-purpose computer.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because a traffic-light controller is a special-purpose computer.
concept: By purpose, computers are general-purpose or special-purpose. A general-purpose computer (such as a PC) can run word processors, games, browsers and many other programs. A special-purpose computer is built for one job, such as controlling traffic lights, a washing machine or a missile; most embedded systems are special-purpose.
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is also true, so 'I only' is incomplete.
B — Correct. I and II are true; III is false because a traffic-light controller does only one job.
C — Wrong. III is false, so all three statements cannot be correct.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Seymour Cray, designer of the CDC 6600 and the CRAY-1, is known as the:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Seymour Cray is called the father of supercomputing.
concept: Seymour Cray designed the CDC 6600 (1964), usually called the first supercomputer, and then founded Cray Research, which built the CRAY-1 (1976). Because of these machines he is called the father of supercomputing.
why: A — Wrong. Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, the designers of TCP/IP, are called the fathers of the Internet.
B — Correct. Seymour Cray is the father of supercomputing.
C — Wrong. The computer mouse was invented by Douglas Engelbart.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The processing speed of a supercomputer is usually measured in:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Supercomputer speed is measured in FLOPS (floating-point operations per second), which is not among A–C.
concept: Supercomputer speed is measured in FLOPS, floating-point operations per second, with prefixes such as teraFLOPS (10^12), petaFLOPS (10^15) and exaFLOPS (10^18). The TOP500 list ranks supercomputers by the FLOPS they reach on the LINPACK (HPL) benchmark. MIPS (million instructions per second) is used for ordinary processors.
why: A — Wrong. Bits per second measures data transfer speed on a network or link, not processing speed.
B — Wrong. Dots per inch measures the resolution of printers and scanners.
C — Wrong. Revolutions per minute measures how fast a disk spins, for example a 7,200 rpm hard disk.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. The unit is FLOPS, which is not listed in A–C.
tip: Supercomputer → FLOPS; ordinary CPU → MIPS; printer → dpi/ppm; network → bps.

q: As of the June 2026 TOP500 list, which supercomputer is ranked No. 1 in the world?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: On the June 2026 TOP500 list, China's LineShine took the No. 1 place.
concept: The TOP500 list of the world's fastest supercomputers is published twice a year, in June and November. On the June 2026 list, China's LineShine became No. 1 with about 2.2 exaFLOPS, moving the US system El Capitan to No. 2; Frontier (USA) was No. 3. Rankings change with every list, so always check the latest one.
why: A — Wrong. Frontier (Oak Ridge National Laboratory, USA) was the first exascale system (2022); on the June 2026 list it is No. 3.
B — Wrong. El Capitan (Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, USA) was No. 1 before LineShine arrived; on the June 2026 list it is No. 2.
C — Correct. LineShine (China) is No. 1 on the June 2026 TOP500 list.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: June 2026 TOP500: 1 LineShine (China), 2 El Capitan (USA), 3 Frontier (USA).

q:
Consider the following statements about supercomputers:
I. Frontier (USA) was the first supercomputer on the TOP500 list to cross the exascale mark (10^18 FLOPS).
II. JUPITER (Germany) is Europe's first exascale supercomputer.
III. The TOP500 list ranks supercomputers by their speed in MIPS.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because the TOP500 ranks systems by FLOPS on the LINPACK (HPL) benchmark.
concept: Exascale means at least 10^18 floating-point operations per second (1 exaFLOPS). Frontier, at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, USA, was the first system on the TOP500 list to pass this mark, in May 2022. JUPITER, at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Germany, became Europe's first exascale system when it reached 1 exaFLOPS on the November 2025 TOP500 list; on the June 2026 list (JUPITER Booster) it is No. 5. The TOP500 ranks systems by FLOPS measured with the LINPACK (HPL) benchmark.
why: A — Correct. Statements I and II are true and III is false.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: the TOP500 uses FLOPS, not MIPS.
C — Wrong. III is false, so all three statements cannot be correct.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Exascale systems on the June 2026 TOP500 list: LineShine (China), El Capitan, Frontier and Aurora (USA), and JUPITER Booster (Germany). First exascale = Frontier (2022); Europe's first = JUPITER (2025).

q: Who led the development of PARAM 8000 (1991) and is known as the father of Indian supercomputing?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Dr Vijay Bhatkar led the C-DAC team that built PARAM 8000.
concept: When India found it hard to import a supercomputer in the late 1980s, the government set up C-DAC (Centre for Development of Advanced Computing) in Pune in 1988. Its team, led by Dr Vijay Bhatkar, built PARAM 8000 in 1991, India's first supercomputer, using parallel processing. 'Param' means 'supreme' in Sanskrit.
why: A — Correct. Vijay Bhatkar is called the father of Indian supercomputing.
B — Wrong. Homi J. Bhabha is the father of India's nuclear programme and founded TIFR (1945).
C — Wrong. APJ Abdul Kalam led India's missile programme and later became President; he did not build PARAM 8000.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following are Indian supercomputers?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Pratyush, Mihir and AIRAWAT are all Indian supercomputers, so more than one option is true.
concept: Pratyush (at IITM, Pune) and Mihir (at NCMRWF, Noida) were dedicated in 2018 for weather and climate forecasting. AIRAWAT (2023), at C-DAC Pune, is India's AI supercomputer. Other Indian systems include PARAM Siddhi-AI (2020) and the PARAM Rudra systems (2024) built under the National Supercomputing Mission.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Pratyush at IITM Pune is used for weather and climate research.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Mihir at NCMRWF Noida is used for weather forecasting.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. AIRAWAT at C-DAC Pune is India's AI supercomputer.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all Indian supercomputers, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Pratyush and Mihir (2018) = weather; AIRAWAT (2023) = AI; PARAM Rudra (2024) = National Supercomputing Mission.

q:
Arrange these milestones of Indian supercomputing in chronological order (earliest first):
1. National Supercomputing Mission launched
2. PARAM 8000 released
3. PARAM Rudra supercomputers dedicated to the nation
4. C-DAC set up in Pune
opts: More than one of the above
exp: C-DAC (1988) → PARAM 8000 (1991) → National Supercomputing Mission (2015) → PARAM Rudra (2024), which is 4, 2, 1, 3.
concept: Timeline: C-DAC set up in Pune (1988) → PARAM 8000, India's first supercomputer (1991) → National Supercomputing Mission launched to build a national grid of supercomputers (2015) → PARAM Rudra systems dedicated to the nation (2024).
why: A — Wrong. PARAM 8000 (1991) was built by C-DAC, so it cannot come before C-DAC was set up (1988).
B — Wrong. It puts PARAM Rudra (2024) before the National Supercomputing Mission (2015), under which it was built.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: In diagrams, a digital signal is usually drawn as a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A digital signal jumps between fixed levels (such as 0 and 1), so it is drawn as a square wave.
concept: An analog signal changes smoothly and continuously, so it is drawn as a sine wave or another smooth curve. A digital signal has only a few fixed levels (in binary, two: 0 and 1) and jumps between them, so it is drawn as a square wave.
why: A — Wrong. A smooth sine wave is how an analog signal is drawn.
B — Correct. A digital signal is drawn as a square wave.
C — Wrong. A continuous curve with no jumps describes an analog signal.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT a property of digital signals?
opts: They are less affected by noise than analog signals
They can represent data as 0s and 1s
More than one of the above
exp: All three are true properties of digital signals, so none of A–C satisfies the NOT stem.
concept: A digital signal takes only a few discrete values, usually two (0 and 1). Because the receiver only has to decide between these levels, small amounts of noise do not change the data, so digital signals are more reliable and less affected by noise than analog signals. Analog signals take continuous values and are measured by amplitude, frequency and phase.
why: A — Wrong. Taking discrete values is a true property of digital signals, so it does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. Being less affected by noise is a true property of digital signals.
C — Wrong. Representing data as 0s and 1s is a true property of digital signals.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. A, B and C are all properties of digital signals, so none of them is 'NOT' a property.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Converting digital data into an analog signal for sending over a telephone line is called modulation.
II. A modem performs both modulation and demodulation.
III. Demodulation converts analog voice into digital form for sending over a digital channel.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because demodulation is done at the receiving end of an analog link, while analog voice is digitised by sampling and quantisation.
concept: A modem (MOdulator–DEModulator) lets digital computers talk over analog lines. At the sender it modulates: it changes a carrier wave to carry the digital bits. At the receiver it demodulates: it recovers the bits from the analog signal. Sending analog voice over a digital channel is a different job, called digitisation (sampling and quantisation, as in PCM).
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is also true, so 'I only' is incomplete.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: analog voice is converted to digital by sampling and quantisation, not by demodulation.
C — Correct. Statements I and II are true and III is false.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: some notes say analog data goes over a digital channel by 'demodulation'. The correct process is digitisation (sampling and quantisation, as in PCM).

q: To send analog data such as a human voice over a digital channel, the signal is first converted by:
opts: Sampling and quantisation (digitisation, as in PCM)
More than one of the above
exp: Analog data is digitised: it is sampled, each sample is rounded to a fixed level (quantised), and the levels are coded in binary.
concept: Digitisation turns an analog signal into numbers. The signal is measured (sampled) at regular intervals, each sample is rounded to one of a fixed set of levels (quantisation), and each level is written as a binary code. This method is called pulse code modulation (PCM), and the device that does it for voice is called a codec (coder–decoder).
why: A — Correct. Sampling and quantisation (PCM) convert analog data into digital form.
B — Wrong. Demodulation is done at the receiving end of an analog link (for example in a modem) to recover digital bits from a modulated carrier; it does not digitise voice.
C — Wrong. Compilation translates a high-level source program into machine code; it has nothing to do with signals.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: some notes call this step 'demodulation'. The correct answer is digitisation: sampling + quantisation + coding (PCM).

q: Which of the following are naturally analog signals?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A human voice and a bird's chirp are natural analog signals; binary data in RAM is digital.
concept: Natural sounds such as speech, birdsong and music are analog: the air pressure changes smoothly and continuously over time. Data inside a computer, such as the contents of RAM, is stored as discrete binary digits (0 and 1), so it is digital.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The human voice is a continuously varying sound wave.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A bird's chirp is also a continuously varying sound wave.
C — Wrong. Binary data stored in RAM consists of discrete 0s and 1s, so it is digital, not analog.
D — Correct. A and B are both analog signals, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which part of the CPU carries out comparisons such as 'Is A greater than B?'
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Comparisons are logical operations, and the ALU performs them.
concept: The ALU performs arithmetic operations (add, subtract, multiply, divide) and logical operations (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, and comparisons such as equal to, greater than, less than). The result of a comparison is recorded in the flag register and is used by the control unit to decide whether to branch.
why: A — Correct. The ALU carries out comparisons.
B — Wrong. The control unit directs and coordinates operations, but it does not itself compare or calculate.
C — Wrong. The program counter is a register that holds the address of the next instruction; it does no comparisons.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which unit of the CPU fetches and decodes instructions and sends control signals to the other parts of the computer?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and generates control signals.
concept: The control unit (CU) is like a manager or a traffic police officer: it does not calculate, but it reads each instruction, decodes it and sends timing and control signals so that memory, the ALU and the input/output devices do the right thing at the right time.
why: A — Wrong. The ALU performs arithmetic and logic; it does not decode instructions or direct other units.
B — Correct. The control unit fetches, decodes and controls.
C — Wrong. The accumulator is a register that holds data for the ALU; it does not send control signals.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: CU = manager (directs); ALU = calculator (computes); registers = the CPU's scratch pad (stores).

q: Which register holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The Program Counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction; it is not among A–C.
concept: The Program Counter (PC), called the Instruction Pointer (IP) in Intel x86, holds the address of the next instruction. After each fetch it is normally increased to point to the following instruction; a jump or branch instruction loads it with a new address.
why: A — Wrong. The IR holds the instruction itself (the one being decoded and executed), not the address of the next one.
B — Wrong. The MDR holds the data or instruction being moved to or from memory, not an address.
C — Wrong. The accumulator holds operands and results of ALU operations.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. The answer is the Program Counter, which is not listed in A–C.
tip: PC = address of the NEXT instruction; IR = the CURRENT instruction itself.

q: Which register holds the instruction that is currently being decoded and executed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The Instruction Register holds the current instruction while the control unit decodes and executes it.
concept: During the fetch step, the instruction is copied from memory into the Instruction Register (IR). The control unit's decoder reads the IR to find out which operation to perform (the opcode) and on what data (the operands).
why: A — Wrong. The MAR holds the address of the memory location being accessed, not the instruction.
B — Wrong. The PC holds the address of the next instruction, not the current instruction itself.
C — Correct. The IR holds the current instruction.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which register holds the address of the memory location that the CPU is about to read from or write to?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The MAR holds the address of the memory location being accessed.
concept: The MAR holds an address; the MDR (also called the Memory Buffer Register, MBR) holds the data word being read from or written to that address. The MAR is connected to the address bus and the MDR to the data bus.
why: A — Correct. The MAR holds the memory address.
B — Wrong. The MDR holds the data being transferred, not the address.
C — Wrong. The IR holds the current instruction, not a memory address to access.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: MAR → Address (address bus); MDR/MBR → Data (data bus).

q: Which of the following are flags commonly found in a CPU's status (flag) register?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Zero, carry and overflow are all standard status flags, so more than one option is true.
concept: The status (flag) register holds single-bit flags that the ALU sets after an operation: Zero (the result was 0), Carry (a carry or borrow came out of the top bit), Sign (the result is negative), Overflow (a signed result was too large), and in some CPUs Parity and Auxiliary carry. Branch instructions test these flags.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The zero flag is set when a result is 0.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The carry flag is set when there is a carry or borrow out of the most significant bit.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The overflow flag is set when a signed result is too large to fit.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all status flags, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT a job of the ALU?
opts: Performing logical AND and OR operations
More than one of the above
exp: Decoding instructions is the job of the control unit, not the ALU.
concept: The ALU does arithmetic (addition, subtraction, and in many CPUs multiplication and division) and logic (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, comparisons, shifts). The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and tells the ALU which operation to perform.
why: A — Wrong. Adding binary numbers is a basic ALU job, so it does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Correct. Decoding instructions is done by the control unit, so it is NOT an ALU job.
C — Wrong. Logical AND and OR are basic ALU operations.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A control unit that produces control signals by reading microinstructions stored in a special control memory is called a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A microprogrammed control unit stores its control steps as microinstructions in control memory.
concept: There are two ways to design a control unit. A hardwired control unit produces control signals with fixed logic circuits (gates, flip-flops, decoders). A microprogrammed control unit stores a microprogram (a sequence of microinstructions) in a control memory, usually ROM, and reads it to produce the signals. Maurice Wilkes proposed microprogramming in 1951.
why: A — Wrong. A hardwired control unit uses fixed logic circuits, not stored microinstructions.
B — Wrong. There is no standard control-unit type called an 'arithmetic control unit'; arithmetic is done by the ALU.
C — Correct. This is a microprogrammed control unit.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. A hardwired control unit is generally faster than a microprogrammed one.
II. A microprogrammed control unit is easier to modify, because its microprogram can be changed.
III. A hardwired control unit stores its control steps as microinstructions in a control memory.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III describes a microprogrammed control unit, not a hardwired one.
concept: Hardwired control: fixed logic circuits, fast, but hard to change or extend; used in RISC processors. Microprogrammed control: microinstructions in control memory, a little slower, but easy to change and good for large instruction sets; traditionally used in CISC processors.
why: A — Correct. Statements I and II are true and III is false.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: storing microinstructions in control memory is what a microprogrammed unit does.
C — Wrong. III is false, so all three statements cannot be correct.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: In many simple CPUs, which register holds the intermediate results of arithmetic and logic operations?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The accumulator holds an operand before an ALU operation and receives the result after it.
concept: The accumulator (ACC, or register A in the Intel 8085) is a special register that holds one operand for the ALU and receives the result, so results build up ('accumulate') in it. In the 8085, most arithmetic and logic instructions use the accumulator.
why: A — Correct. The accumulator holds intermediate results.
B — Wrong. The program counter holds the address of the next instruction, not data results.
C — Wrong. The MAR holds the address of the memory location being accessed, not ALU results.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which storage locations are the fastest in a computer and are located inside the CPU itself?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Registers are built into the CPU and are the fastest storage in the computer.
concept: Registers are tiny storage cells, typically 8 to 64 bits each, built into the CPU. The CPU can read and write them within a single clock cycle, so they are at the top of the memory hierarchy: fastest, smallest and most costly per bit. Registers are volatile.
why: A — Wrong. RAM is main memory outside the CPU; it is much slower than registers and cache.
B — Correct. Registers are the fastest storage and are inside the CPU.
C — Wrong. A hard disk is secondary storage outside the CPU and is far slower.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT a job of the CPU?
opts: Controlling and coordinating the other units
Storing files permanently when the power is off
More than one of the above
exp: Permanent storage of files is done by secondary storage such as hard disks and SSDs, not by the CPU.
concept: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is called the brain of the computer because it processes data (in the ALU) and controls all other units (through the control unit). Permanent storage is the job of secondary storage such as hard disks and SSDs; the CPU's registers lose their contents when the power goes off.
why: A — Wrong. Processing data is a main job of the CPU, so it does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. Controlling the other units is a main job of the CPU (done by its control unit).
C — Correct. Storing files permanently is NOT a CPU job; it belongs to secondary storage.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following are parts of the CPU?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The ALU, the control unit and the registers are all parts of the CPU, so more than one option is true.
concept: A CPU has three main parts: the ALU (calculations and comparisons), the control unit (directs operations) and registers (very fast storage for the data and instructions being worked on). Many Indian books list the parts as ALU, CU and memory unit, where the memory unit means the registers. Modern CPU chips also contain cache memory.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The ALU is the part of the CPU that calculates and compares.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The control unit is the part of the CPU that directs all operations.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Registers are the CPU's own small, fast storage cells.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all parts of the CPU, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The control unit does not process data itself; it directs the other units.
II. The ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations.
III. The program counter stores the result of the last ALU operation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because the program counter holds the address of the next instruction, not ALU results.
