concept: Jobs inside the CPU: the control unit fetches and decodes instructions and directs the other units; the ALU does arithmetic and logic; registers hold data, addresses and instructions. The program counter holds the address of the next instruction, while results of ALU operations go to the accumulator or another general-purpose register.
why: A — Correct. Statements I and II are true and III is false.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: ALU results go to the accumulator or another register, not to the program counter.
C — Wrong. III is false, so all three statements cannot be correct.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT a CPU register?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: PC, MAR and the accumulator are all CPU registers, so none of A–C satisfies the NOT stem.
concept: Common CPU registers: Program Counter (address of the next instruction), Instruction Register (current instruction), MAR (memory address), MDR or MBR (memory data), Accumulator (operand and result for the ALU), Stack Pointer (top of the stack), flag or status register, and general-purpose registers.
why: A — Wrong. The program counter is a CPU register, so it does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. The MAR is a CPU register that holds a memory address.
C — Wrong. The accumulator is a CPU register that holds ALU operands and results.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. A, B and C are all CPU registers, so none of them is 'NOT' a register.

q: Which type of control unit has traditionally been used in CISC processors, because it handles a large and complex instruction set more easily?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: CISC processors have traditionally used microprogrammed control, because complex instructions are easier to write as microprograms.
concept: CISC processors such as the Intel x86 family have hundreds of instructions, many of which need several steps. Writing these steps as microprograms is easier than designing fixed logic circuits for each one, so CISC processors traditionally use microprogrammed control. RISC processors have a few simple instructions and use hardwired control for speed.
why: A — Wrong. Hardwired control is typical of RISC processors, whose few simple instructions suit fixed logic.
B — Correct. Microprogrammed control is traditionally used in CISC processors.
C — Wrong. There is no standard control-unit type called an 'optical control unit'.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: RISC → hardwired control; CISC → microprogrammed control.

q: During the fetch phase of an instruction cycle, which is the correct order of register transfers?
opts: MDR → IR, then PC → MAR, then memory → MDR
PC → MDR, then MDR → MAR, then MAR → IR
PC → MAR, then memory → MDR, then MDR → IR
More than one of the above
exp: The address in PC goes to MAR, memory puts the instruction into MDR, and the instruction then moves from MDR to IR.
concept: Fetch uses four registers. The PC holds the address of the next instruction. The MAR sends that address to memory on the address bus. The word read from memory arrives in the MDR through the data bus. The instruction is then copied into the IR, where the control unit decodes it. The PC is increased so that it points to the next instruction.
why: A — Wrong. It copies MDR into IR before anything has been read from memory, so the IR would get old data.
B — Wrong. The PC holds an address, which must go to the MAR (not the MDR), and moving MAR into IR would put an address, not an instruction, into the IR.
C — Correct. PC → MAR, memory → MDR, MDR → IR is the fetch sequence.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: Step 1: MAR ← PC (the address of the next instruction is placed on the address bus). Step 2: MDR ← Memory[MAR] (memory returns the instruction on the data bus); at the same time PC ← PC + 1 so it points to the next instruction. Step 3: IR ← MDR (the instruction is ready to be decoded by the control unit).

q: Which register points to the top of the stack in memory?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The Stack Pointer (SP) holds the address of the top of the stack.
concept: A stack is an area of memory used in last-in, first-out (LIFO) order, for example to save return addresses during function calls. The Stack Pointer (SP) holds the address of the top of the stack and changes with every PUSH and POP.
why: A — Wrong. The Instruction Register holds the current instruction, not a stack address.
B — Correct. The Stack Pointer points to the top of the stack.
C — Wrong. The MDR holds the data being moved to or from memory.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The system bus of a computer is made up of:
opts: The data bus, address bus and control bus
The power and ground lines only
More than one of the above
exp: The system bus has three parts: the data bus, the address bus and the control bus.
concept: A bus is a set of parallel wires that carries signals between the CPU, memory and input/output devices. The system bus has three parts: the data bus (carries data), the address bus (carries the address of a memory location or I/O port) and the control bus (carries control signals such as read, write and interrupt).
why: A — Wrong. The data bus is only one of the three parts of the system bus.
B — Correct. The system bus = data bus + address bus + control bus.
C — Wrong. Power and ground lines supply electricity; they do not make up the system bus.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Address bus: one-way (CPU → memory/I/O). Data bus: two-way. Control bus: read/write, interrupt, clock signals.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The data bus is bidirectional.
II. The address bus normally carries addresses in one direction only, from the CPU to memory and I/O devices.
III. The width of the address bus decides the maximum memory the CPU can address directly.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three statements are true.
concept: The data bus is bidirectional because data travels both into the CPU (read) and out of it (write). The address bus is unidirectional: the CPU sends out addresses, and memory or I/O devices receive them. With n address lines the CPU can form 2^n addresses, so the address-bus width sets the largest memory it can address directly.
why: A — Correct. Statements I, II and III are all true.
B — Wrong. 'I and II only' leaves out III, which is also true: n address lines give 2^n addresses.
C — Wrong. 'I only' leaves out II and III, which are also true.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT carried on the control bus?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The memory address travels on the address bus, not the control bus.
concept: The control bus carries signals that coordinate the system: memory read and write, I/O read and write, interrupt request and acknowledge, clock, reset, and bus request and grant. Addresses travel on the address bus, and data travels on the data bus.
why: A — Wrong. Read and write signals are carried on the control bus, so this does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. Interrupt request signals are also carried on the control bus.
C — Correct. The memory address is carried on the address bus, so it is NOT carried on the control bus.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A processor has a 16-bit address bus and its memory is byte-addressable. What is the maximum memory it can address?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 2^16 = 65,536 bytes = 64 KB, which is not among A–C.
concept: With n address lines a CPU can form 2^n different addresses. If each address holds one byte (byte-addressable memory), the maximum memory is 2^n bytes. The Intel 8085 has a 16-bit address bus, so it can address 64 KB.
why: A — Wrong. 16 KB = 2^14 bytes would need only 14 address lines.
B — Wrong. 1 MB = 2^20 bytes needs a 20-bit address bus (as in the 8086).
C — Wrong. 16 MB = 2^24 bytes needs a 24-bit address bus (as in the 80286).
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. The answer is 64 KB, which is not listed in A–C.
work: Number of addresses = 2^16 = 65,536. Each address holds 1 byte, so memory = 65,536 bytes. 65,536 ÷ 1,024 = 64 KB. 64 KB is not among A–C, so the answer is E.
tip: Common mistake: some notes give 1 MB for the 8085. The 8085 (16-bit address bus) addresses 64 KB; 1 MB belongs to the 8086 (20-bit).

q: The Intel 8086 has a 20-bit address bus and byte-addressable memory. How much memory can it address directly?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: Maximum memory = 2^(number of address lines) bytes for byte-addressable memory. Intel examples: 8085 — 16 lines — 64 KB; 8086 — 20 lines — 1 MB; 80286 — 24 lines — 16 MB; 80386 — 32 lines — 4 GB.
why: A — Wrong. 64 KB = 2^16 bytes is the limit of a 16-bit address bus (8085).
B — Correct. A 20-bit address bus gives 2^20 bytes = 1 MB.
C — Wrong. 16 MB = 2^24 bytes is the limit of a 24-bit address bus (80286).
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Address lines → memory: 16 → 64 KB, 20 → 1 MB, 24 → 16 MB, 32 → 4 GB.

q: How many address lines are needed to address 4 GB of byte-addressable memory?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 4 GB = 2^32 bytes, so 32 address lines are needed.
concept: To find the number of address lines, write the memory size in bytes as a power of 2: if memory = 2^n bytes, then n address lines are needed. Useful powers: 2^10 = 1 K, 2^20 = 1 M, 2^30 = 1 G.
why: A — Wrong. 16 address lines give only 2^16 bytes = 64 KB.
B — Wrong. 30 address lines give 2^30 bytes = 1 GB, which is only a quarter of 4 GB.
C — Correct. 32 address lines give 2^32 bytes = 4 GB.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: 4 GB = 4 × 2^30 bytes = 2^2 × 2^30 bytes = 2^32 bytes. Since 2^n = 2^32, n = 32 address lines.

q: A memory chip is organised as 2K × 8 (2,048 locations, each 8 bits wide). How many address lines and data lines does it need?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 2,048 = 2^11 locations need 11 address lines; 8-bit locations need 8 data lines.
concept: A memory chip described as N × M has N locations, each M bits wide. The number of address lines is the power of 2 that gives N (N = 2^n means n lines). The number of data lines equals the width M.
why: A — Correct. 11 address lines (2^11 = 2,048) and 8 data lines.
B — Wrong. It swaps the two numbers: the 8 bits of width need 8 data lines, and the 2,048 locations need 11 address lines.
C — Wrong. It confuses the number of locations with the number of lines; 11 lines are enough to select 2,048 locations because 2^11 = 2,048.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: Locations = 2K = 2 × 1,024 = 2,048 = 2^11, so 11 address lines. Width = 8 bits, so 8 data lines.
tip: For an N × M chip: address lines = log2(N), data lines = M.

q: Which of the following are true of the von Neumann architecture?
opts: Program instructions and data are stored in the same memory
Instructions and data travel over the same bus, so they cannot be fetched at the same time
It is based on the stored-program concept
More than one of the above
exp: All three are true of the von Neumann architecture, so more than one option is true.
concept: In the von Neumann (Princeton) architecture, one memory holds both instructions and data, and one bus path connects it to the CPU. This is simple and flexible, but the CPU can fetch either an instruction or data at one time, so the shared path limits speed; this is called the von Neumann bottleneck. Most general-purpose computers follow this model and use caches to reduce the bottleneck.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. One memory holds both instructions and data.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The shared bus means an instruction and data cannot be fetched together, which is the von Neumann bottleneck.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The program is stored in memory like data, which is the stored-program concept.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of the above is correct.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: An architecture with separate memories and separate buses for instructions and data is called:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Harvard architecture keeps instructions and data in separate memories with separate buses.
concept: Harvard architecture keeps instructions and data in separate memories with separate buses, so the CPU can fetch an instruction and read data at the same time. It is named after the Harvard Mark I. It is common in microcontrollers and digital signal processors (DSPs). Modern PCs use separate L1 instruction and data caches, which is called a modified Harvard design.
why: A — Wrong. The von Neumann architecture uses one memory and one bus path for both instructions and data.
B — Wrong. CISC describes the kind of instruction set (many complex instructions), not separate memories.
C — Correct. This is the Harvard architecture.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of RISC processors?
opts: A large number of complex, variable-length instructions
Most instructions complete in about one clock cycle, which suits pipelining
More than one of the above
exp: Many complex, variable-length instructions are a CISC feature, not a RISC feature.
concept: RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) uses a small set of simple, fixed-length instructions, many registers and a load/store design (only load and store instructions access memory). Most instructions take about one cycle, so pipelining is easy. ARM processors in smartphones are RISC. CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer), such as Intel x86, has many complex, variable-length instructions.
why: A — Correct. Many complex, variable-length instructions describe CISC, so this is NOT a RISC feature.
B — Wrong. Simple fixed-length instructions are a true RISC feature, so this does not satisfy the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. Executing most instructions in about one cycle, which helps pipelining, is a true RISC feature.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: RISC example: ARM (phones). CISC example: Intel/AMD x86 (most PCs).

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Word size is the number of bits a CPU can process as one unit.
II. Clock speed is measured in hertz (for example, GHz).
III. The word size of a 64-bit processor is 8 bytes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three statements are true: 64 bits ÷ 8 = 8 bytes.
concept: Word size is the number of bits the CPU handles in one operation; it usually equals the size of its general-purpose registers (8-bit 8085, 16-bit 8086, 32-bit 80386, 64-bit modern CPUs). A 64-bit word is 64 ÷ 8 = 8 bytes. (In Intel assembly language the data type named WORD is only 16 bits for historical reasons; that name is not the CPU's word size.) Clock speed is the number of clock cycles per second, measured in hertz; modern desktop CPUs run at about 3–6 GHz.
why: A — Wrong. 'I only' leaves out II and III, which are also true.
B — Wrong. 'I and II only' leaves out III, which is also true: 64 bits = 8 bytes.
C — Correct. Statements I, II and III are all true.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: some notes show '34 GHz'. Modern clock speeds are about 3–6 GHz.

q: What is the correct order of the basic steps of the instruction cycle?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: An instruction must first be fetched from memory, then decoded, then executed.
concept: The CPU repeats the instruction cycle (also called the fetch–decode–execute or machine cycle) for every instruction. Fetch brings the instruction from memory into the IR; decode lets the control unit work out what it means; execute carries it out. Some books add a fourth step, store (write back the result).
why: A — Wrong. An instruction cannot be decoded before it has been fetched from memory.
B — Correct. Fetch → Decode → Execute is the order in which every instruction is handled.
C — Wrong. Nothing can be executed before it has been fetched and decoded.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: 1. Fetch: the instruction at the address in the PC is copied from memory into the IR, and the PC is increased. 2. Decode: the control unit reads the opcode in the IR and works out the operation and operands. 3. Execute: the operation is carried out (for example the ALU adds), and the result is stored. The cycle then repeats for the next instruction.

q: A processor's clock runs at 2.5 GHz. How long is one clock cycle?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Cycle time = 1 ÷ (2.5 × 10^9 Hz) = 0.4 ns, which is not among A–C.
concept: The time for one clock cycle (the clock period) is T = 1 / f, where f is the clock frequency. 1 GHz = 10^9 Hz, and 1 ns = 10^-9 s, so a frequency in GHz gives a period in ns: T (ns) = 1 / f (GHz). A higher clock frequency means a shorter cycle.
why: A — Wrong. A 2.5 ns cycle would mean a 400 MHz clock (1 ÷ 2.5 ns).
B — Wrong. A 4 ns cycle would mean a 250 MHz clock.
C — Wrong. A 0.25 ns cycle would mean a 4 GHz clock.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. The cycle time is 0.4 ns, which is not listed in A–C.
work: f = 2.5 GHz = 2.5 × 10^9 Hz. T = 1 / f = 1 / (2.5 × 10^9) s = 0.4 × 10^-9 s = 0.4 ns. 0.4 ns is not among A–C, so the answer is E.
tip: Shortcut: cycle time in ns = 1 ÷ (clock in GHz). 1 GHz → 1 ns, 2 GHz → 0.5 ns, 4 GHz → 0.25 ns.

q: A processor runs at 2 GHz and needs on average 4 clock cycles per instruction (CPI = 4). What is its speed in MIPS?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Instructions per second = 2 × 10^9 ÷ 4 = 500 × 10^6, which is 500 MIPS.
concept: MIPS means millions of instructions per second. MIPS = clock rate ÷ (CPI × 10^6), where CPI is the average number of clock cycles each instruction needs. A higher clock rate or a lower CPI gives a higher MIPS rating.
why: B — Wrong. 8,000 comes from multiplying the clock rate by the CPI instead of dividing by it.
C — Wrong. 2,000 ignores the CPI; it would be right only if each instruction took 1 cycle.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: Instructions per second = clock rate ÷ CPI = (2 × 10^9) ÷ 4 = 0.5 × 10^9 = 500 × 10^6. MIPS = 500 × 10^6 ÷ 10^6 = 500.
tip: Shortcut: MIPS = clock in MHz ÷ CPI. Here 2,000 MHz ÷ 4 = 500 MIPS.

q: Which of the following are true of a multi-core processor?
opts: It has two or more processing units (cores) on a single chip
It can run several threads or tasks truly in parallel
Each core usually has its own L1 cache
More than one of the above
exp: All three are true of multi-core processors, so more than one option is true.
concept: A multi-core processor places two or more independent cores on one chip. Each core can run its own thread, so the processor can do several tasks at the same moment (true parallelism). Each core usually has a private L1 cache (and often a private L2), while the L3 cache is commonly shared by all cores. Dual-core, quad-core and octa-core chips are common in PCs and phones.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A multi-core chip contains two or more cores.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each core can run a separate thread, so tasks run truly in parallel.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each core normally has its own private L1 cache.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of the above is correct.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which order arranges memory from fastest to slowest?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Registers are fastest, then cache, then main memory (RAM), then secondary storage such as a hard disk.
concept: Memory hierarchy from top to bottom: registers → cache (L1, L2, L3) → main memory (RAM) → secondary storage (SSD, hard disk) → offline storage (magnetic tape, optical discs). Speed and cost per bit fall as we go down; capacity rises.
why: A — Wrong. Registers, inside the CPU, are faster than cache.
B — Wrong. RAM is slower than both cache and registers.
C — Correct. Registers → cache → RAM → hard disk is fastest to slowest.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: As we move down the memory hierarchy (from registers towards the hard disk), which of the following does NOT happen?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Going down the hierarchy, cost per bit decreases; it does not increase.
concept: Memory hierarchy (top to bottom): registers → cache → main memory (RAM) → secondary storage (SSD/HDD) → offline storage (tape, optical discs). Going down, capacity increases, cost per bit decreases and access time increases (the memory gets slower). Going up, the opposite is true.
why: A — Correct. Cost per bit decreases going down, so 'cost per bit increases' does NOT happen.
B — Wrong. Capacity does increase going down (a hard disk holds far more than the registers), so this does not satisfy the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. Access time does increase going down; lower levels are slower.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Down the pyramid: bigger, cheaper per bit, slower. Up the pyramid: smaller, costlier per bit, faster.

q: Static RAM (SRAM) stores each bit in a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SRAM stores each bit in a flip-flop (latch), so it needs no refreshing.
concept: SRAM uses a flip-flop of usually six transistors per bit; it keeps the bit as long as the power is on, with no refreshing. It is fast but costly and takes more space, so it is used for cache. DRAM uses one transistor and one capacitor per bit; the charge leaks away, so DRAM must be refreshed many times a second. DRAM is cheaper and denser, so it is used for main memory.
why: A — Wrong. A capacitor that must be refreshed describes DRAM, not SRAM.
B — Correct. SRAM uses a transistor flip-flop for each bit.
C — Wrong. Magnetised spots are how a hard disk stores bits; RAM is semiconductor memory.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: SRAM: flip-flop, no refresh, fast, costly → cache. DRAM: capacitor, needs refresh, cheaper, denser → main memory.

q: Which of the following are true of dynamic RAM (DRAM)?
opts: It stores each bit as a charge on a capacitor
It is commonly used as main memory
More than one of the above
exp: All three are true of DRAM, so more than one option is true.
concept: DRAM stores each bit as an electric charge on a tiny capacitor, controlled by one transistor. The charge leaks away within milliseconds, so the memory controller refreshes every row many times a second. Because each cell is so small, DRAM is cheap and dense, which makes it the usual choice for main memory (for example DDR4 and DDR5 modules).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. DRAM stores each bit as a charge on a capacitor.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Because the charge leaks, DRAM must be refreshed periodically.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. DRAM is cheap and dense, so it is used for main memory.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of the above is correct.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT volatile memory?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SRAM, DRAM and L1 cache all lose their contents without power, so all three are volatile.
concept: Volatile memory loses its contents when the power is switched off. Registers, cache (built from SRAM) and main memory (DRAM) are all volatile. Non-volatile memory keeps its data without power: ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash memory, hard disks, SSDs and optical discs.
why: A — Wrong. SRAM keeps data only while power is supplied, so it is volatile and does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. DRAM is volatile; it even needs refreshing while the power is on.
C — Wrong. L1 cache is made of SRAM, so it is volatile.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. All three are volatile, so none of them is 'NOT volatile'.
tip: Volatile = needs power to keep data: registers, cache, RAM. Non-volatile: ROM family, flash, disks.

q: The main purpose of cache memory in a CPU is to:
opts: Increase the capacity of the hard disk
Reduce the average time the CPU waits for data from main memory
More than one of the above
exp: Cache keeps copies of frequently used data close to the CPU, so most accesses avoid slow main memory.
concept: Main memory (DRAM) is much slower than the CPU. Cache is a small, fast SRAM memory between the CPU and main memory that holds copies of recently and frequently used instructions and data. When the CPU finds what it needs in the cache, it does not have to wait for main memory, so the average access time falls.
why: A — Wrong. Cache is volatile and very small; permanent storage of files is the job of secondary storage.
B — Wrong. CPU cache does not add capacity to the hard disk; it speeds up access to main memory.
C — Correct. Cache reduces the average time the CPU waits for memory.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which level of cache is the smallest and fastest?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: L1 cache is the smallest and fastest cache level, closest to the CPU core.
concept: L1 cache is inside each core, very small (tens of KB) and the fastest; it is often split into an instruction cache and a data cache. L2 is larger and a little slower. L3 is the largest and slowest cache level and is usually shared by all cores. All cache levels are faster than main memory.
why: A — Correct. L1 is the smallest and fastest cache.
B — Wrong. L2 is larger and slower than L1.
C — Wrong. L3 is the largest and slowest cache level, usually shared by all cores.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: DDR SDRAM is called 'double data rate' because it:
opts: Uses two memory chips for every bit
Transfers data on both the rising and the falling edges of the clock
Runs at double the supply voltage of SDRAM
More than one of the above
exp: DDR transfers data twice in each clock cycle, on the rising edge and on the falling edge.
concept: Synchronous DRAM (SDRAM) works in step with the system clock and transfers data once per clock cycle. DDR SDRAM transfers data twice per cycle, on both the rising and falling edges of the clock, which doubles the data rate at the same clock speed. Later versions (DDR2, DDR3, DDR4, DDR5) raised the speed further and lowered the supply voltage.
why: A — Wrong. DDR does not use two chips per bit; the doubling comes from using both clock edges.
B — Correct. Data moves on both the rising and the falling clock edges.
C — Wrong. DDR memories actually use lower supply voltages than older SDRAM, not double.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Virtual memory lets a computer run programs larger than its RAM by using part of:
opts: The secondary storage (hard disk or SSD)
More than one of the above
exp: Virtual memory uses an area of secondary storage (a page file or swap space) as an extension of RAM.
concept: With virtual memory the operating system uses an area of secondary storage, called a page file or swap space, as an extension of RAM. Programs are divided into pages; pages not in use are kept on the disk and brought into RAM when needed (paging). This lets bigger or more programs run, but the disk is much slower than RAM, so too much swapping slows the computer (thrashing).
why: A — Wrong. Cache is smaller than RAM, so it cannot be used to make memory look larger.
B — Correct. Virtual memory uses part of the hard disk or SSD.
C — Wrong. ROM is read-only, so it cannot hold the pages that programs write to.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The small CMOS memory on a PC motherboard keeps BIOS settings such as the date, time and boot order. What keeps it powered when the computer is switched off?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A coin-cell battery on the motherboard keeps the CMOS memory and the real-time clock running.
concept: CMOS (Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor) memory is a small, low-power RAM that stores BIOS/UEFI settings and works with the real-time clock. Because it is volatile, a coin-cell battery (often a CR2032) keeps it powered. If the battery dies, the PC forgets the date and time and its settings go back to the defaults.
why: A — Correct. The CMOS battery keeps the settings alive.
B — Wrong. A hard disk is a storage device; it does not supply power to other chips.
C — Wrong. Ultraviolet light is used to erase EPROM chips; it does not power anything.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: BIOS ≠ CMOS: BIOS is the start-up program kept in ROM/flash; CMOS is the small battery-backed memory that keeps its settings.

q: Which of the following are true of main memory (RAM)?
opts: The CPU can access it directly
Any location can be reached in about the same time, which is why it is called 'random access'
More than one of the above
exp: All three are true of RAM, so more than one option is true.
concept: RAM (Random Access Memory) is the computer's main or primary memory. It holds the programs and data in current use, and the CPU reads and writes it directly over the system bus. 'Random access' means any location can be reached in about the same time, unlike a tape, which must be read in order. RAM is volatile, so its contents are lost when the power goes off.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The CPU reads and writes RAM directly; secondary storage must first be loaded into RAM.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Every RAM location takes about the same time to reach, which is the meaning of 'random access'.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. RAM loses its contents when the power is switched off.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of the above is correct.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Cache memory is slower than CPU registers.
II. In multi-core processors, the L3 cache is usually shared by all cores.
III. SRAM must be refreshed periodically to keep its data.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because SRAM keeps its data without refreshing as long as power is on (DRAM needs refreshing).
concept: Registers are the fastest storage, then the cache levels (L1 fastest, L3 slowest), then main memory. In multi-core chips, L1 and usually L2 are private to each core, while L3 is shared. SRAM uses flip-flops and needs no refresh; DRAM uses capacitors and must be refreshed.
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is also true, so 'I only' is incomplete.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: it is DRAM, not SRAM, that must be refreshed.
C — Correct. Statements I and II are true and III is false.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: When the data the CPU needs is found in the cache, it is called a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Finding the requested data in the cache is called a cache hit.
concept: If the requested data is in the cache, it is a cache hit and the data arrives quickly. If it is not, it is a cache miss: the data must come from slower main memory and is usually copied into the cache. Hit ratio = number of hits ÷ total number of accesses. A page fault is a different event in virtual memory: a needed page is not in RAM and must be loaded from disk.
why: A — Wrong. A cache miss means the data was NOT found in the cache.
B — Correct. Finding the data in the cache is a cache hit.
C — Wrong. A page fault happens in virtual memory when a page is not in RAM; it has nothing to do with finding data in the cache.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Hit = found in cache; miss = not in cache; page fault = page not in RAM (virtual memory).

q: A cache has a hit ratio of 0.9. A hit takes 10 ns, and a miss takes 100 ns in total. What is the average memory access time?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: Average access time is a weighted average: (hit ratio × time for a hit) + (miss ratio × time for a miss), where miss ratio = 1 − hit ratio. A high hit ratio keeps the average close to the fast cache time, which is why caches work so well.
why: B — Wrong. 55 ns is the simple average (10 + 100) ÷ 2, which ignores how often hits and misses happen.
C — Wrong. 91 ns swaps the weights: it uses 0.9 for the miss time and 0.1 for the hit time.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: Miss ratio = 1 − 0.9 = 0.1. Average time = (0.9 × 10 ns) + (0.1 × 100 ns) = 9 ns + 10 ns = 19 ns.

q: Programs tend to reuse recently used data and to access nearby addresses ('locality of reference'). This is the main reason why which memory works well?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Cache keeps recently used blocks near the CPU, and locality of reference makes those blocks likely to be needed again.
concept: Locality of reference has two forms: temporal locality (an item used recently is likely to be used again soon, such as a loop variable) and spatial locality (items near a recently used address are likely to be used soon, such as the next elements of an array). Cache keeps recently used blocks close to the CPU, so most accesses become fast cache hits.
why: A — Wrong. ROM holds fixed firmware; it does not keep copies of recently used data.
B — Correct. Cache memory works well because of locality of reference.
C — Wrong. Magnetic tape is slow, sequential-access storage; locality of reference is not what makes it useful.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which type of ROM has its contents written by the manufacturer during chip fabrication, so they can never be changed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Mask ROM is programmed at the factory and cannot be changed afterwards.
concept: Mask ROM (masked ROM) is programmed at the factory with a photomask while the chip is being made. It is cheap in very large quantities but can never be changed. PROM is written once by the user; EPROM can be erased with UV light and rewritten; EEPROM and flash memory can be erased electrically.
why: A — Correct. Mask ROM is written during manufacture and is permanent.
B — Wrong. EPROM can be erased with ultraviolet light and programmed again.
C — Wrong. EEPROM can be erased electrically and programmed again.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: How many times can a user program a PROM (Programmable ROM) chip?
opts: Never; only the factory can program it
More than one of the above
exp: A PROM can be programmed by the user only once.
concept: A PROM is made blank, and the user writes data into it once with a device called a PROM programmer (or burner), usually by blowing tiny fuses inside the chip. After that it cannot be changed, which is why it is also called OTP (one-time programmable) ROM.
why: A — Wrong. A PROM cannot be erased, so it cannot be programmed again and again (EPROM and EEPROM can).
B — Correct. A PROM is one-time programmable.
C — Wrong. That describes mask ROM; a PROM is made to be programmed by the user.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following can NOT be erased electrically?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: EPROM is erased with ultraviolet light, not electrically.
concept: EPROM (Erasable Programmable ROM) has a small quartz window on top of the chip. It is erased by shining strong ultraviolet (UV) light through the window for several minutes, which wipes the whole chip; it can then be programmed again. EEPROM and flash memory are erased by electrical signals while they stay in the circuit.
why: A — Wrong. EEPROM means Electrically Erasable PROM, so it can be erased electrically and does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. Flash memory is a kind of EEPROM and is erased electrically, block by block.
C — Correct. EPROM is erased by UV light, so it can NOT be erased electrically.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: EPROM → UV light, whole chip. EEPROM → electrically, byte by byte. Flash → electrically, block by block.

q: How is the data in an EEPROM chip erased?
opts: By exposing the chip to ultraviolet light
It cannot be erased once written
More than one of the above
exp: EEPROM is erased electrically, byte by byte, which is not among A–C.
concept: EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable ROM) is erased and rewritten with electrical signals, one byte at a time, without removing the chip from the circuit. It is used to store small amounts of settings data. Flash memory is a kind of EEPROM that erases larger blocks at once, which makes it faster and cheaper for large storage.
why: A — Wrong. Ultraviolet light is used to erase EPROM, not EEPROM.
B — Wrong. Magnetic fields are used with magnetic media such as tapes and hard disks, not semiconductor ROM.
C — Wrong. That describes mask ROM or a programmed PROM; EEPROM is made to be erased.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. EEPROM is erased electrically, which is not listed in A–C.

q: Which of the following are true of flash memory?
opts: It is a type of EEPROM that is erased in blocks
It is used in pen drives, memory cards and SSDs
More than one of the above
exp: All three are true of flash memory, so more than one option is true.
concept: Flash memory is a non-volatile semiconductor memory developed from EEPROM. Instead of erasing one byte at a time, it erases a whole block at once, which makes it fast and cheap for large capacities. It is used in pen drives, SD and microSD cards, SSDs, smartphones, and to hold the BIOS/UEFI firmware of modern PCs.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Flash memory keeps its data without power.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Flash is a kind of EEPROM that erases whole blocks at once.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Pen drives, memory cards and SSDs are all built from flash memory.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of the above is correct.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT a type of ROM?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SDRAM (Synchronous Dynamic RAM) is volatile main memory, not ROM.
concept: Types of ROM: mask ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM and flash memory (a kind of EEPROM). All are non-volatile. SDRAM is synchronous dynamic RAM, the volatile main memory of computers; DDR SDRAM is its faster form.
why: A — Correct. SDRAM is a type of RAM, so it is NOT a type of ROM.
B — Wrong. PROM (Programmable ROM) is a type of ROM, so it does not satisfy the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. EPROM (Erasable Programmable ROM) is a type of ROM.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. ROM is non-volatile memory.
II. An EEPROM can be erased and rewritten byte by byte while it stays in the circuit.
III. A mask ROM can be reprogrammed by the user.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because mask ROM is fixed at the factory and can never be changed.
concept: All types of ROM keep their data without power. They differ in how they are written and erased: mask ROM — written at the factory, never changed; PROM — written once by the user; EPROM — erased by UV light; EEPROM — erased electrically, byte by byte, in the circuit; flash — erased electrically, block by block.
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is also true, so 'I only' is incomplete.
B — Correct. Statements I and II are true and III is false.
C — Wrong. III is false, so all three statements cannot be correct.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: In most modern PCs, the BIOS/UEFI firmware is stored in:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Modern PCs keep their BIOS/UEFI firmware in flash memory, a rewritable kind of ROM (EEPROM).
concept: BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) and its modern replacement UEFI are firmware that run first when a PC starts: they test the hardware (POST) and then load the operating system. The firmware must survive power-off, so it is kept in non-volatile ROM-type memory. Older PCs used mask ROM, PROM or EPROM chips; modern PCs use flash memory, so the BIOS can be updated ('flashed').
why: A — Wrong. DRAM is volatile, so it would lose the BIOS every time the power went off.
B — Wrong. Cache memory is volatile SRAM inside the CPU; it cannot keep firmware without power.
C — Correct. Modern BIOS/UEFI firmware is stored in flash memory.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Books often say 'BIOS is stored in ROM'. Flash is a rewritable kind of ROM (EEPROM), so both statements agree.

q: Blu-ray discs are read with a laser of which colour and wavelength?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Blu-ray uses a blue-violet laser of 405 nm, which gives the format its name.
concept: Optical discs are read by lasers. A shorter wavelength makes a smaller spot, so data can be packed more densely. CD: infrared, about 780 nm, about 700 MB. DVD: red, about 650 nm, 4.7 GB single layer. Blu-ray: blue-violet, 405 nm, 25 GB single layer and 50 GB dual layer.
why: A — Wrong. An infrared laser of about 780 nm is used for CDs.
B — Wrong. A red laser of about 650 nm is used for DVDs.
C — Correct. Blu-ray uses a blue-violet 405 nm laser.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Shorter wavelength → more capacity: CD 780 nm (700 MB) → DVD 650 nm (4.7 GB) → Blu-ray 405 nm (25 GB).

q: Which of the following capacity pairs is NOT correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three pairs are correct, so none of A–C satisfies the NOT stem.
concept: Standard optical disc capacities: CD 650–700 MB; DVD 4.7 GB (single layer) and 8.5 GB (dual layer); Blu-ray 25 GB (single layer) and 50 GB (dual layer). A 3.5-inch floppy disk holds 1.44 MB.
why: A — Wrong. A CD holds about 650–700 MB, so this pair is correct and does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. A single-layer DVD holds 4.7 GB, so this pair is correct.
C — Wrong. A single-layer Blu-ray disc holds 25 GB, so this pair is correct.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. All three pairs are correct, so none of them is 'NOT correct'.

q: Which of the following is NOT an optical storage device?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A hard disk drive stores data magnetically, not optically.
concept: Secondary storage is grouped by technology. Magnetic: hard disk drive, magnetic tape, floppy disk. Optical (read by laser): CD, DVD, Blu-ray. Solid-state (flash memory): SSD, pen drive, memory card.
why: A — Wrong. A CD-ROM is read by a laser, so it is optical and does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Correct. A hard disk drive is magnetic storage, so it is NOT optical.
C — Wrong. A Blu-ray disc is read by a blue-violet laser, so it is optical.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following storage devices can access data only sequentially (in order, from the beginning)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Sequential-only access is a feature of magnetic tape, which is not among A–C.
concept: Sequential access means reaching a record only after passing all the records before it, like a cassette tape; magnetic tape is the standard example (a sequential access storage device, SASD). Direct (random) access means going straight to any record; hard disks, SSDs, CDs, DVDs and pen drives are direct access storage devices (DASD).
why: A — Wrong. A hard disk is a direct access device: the head can move straight to any track and sector.
B — Wrong. An SSD reaches any block directly by its address; it has no moving parts at all.
C — Wrong. A pen drive is flash memory; like an SSD, it reaches any block directly by its address, so it is a direct access device.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fits the question, so more than one of them cannot.
E — Correct. Only magnetic tape is sequential-access, and it is not listed in A–C.
tip: Tape = sequential access (SASD). Hard disk, SSD, CD/DVD = direct access (DASD).

q: A hard disk has 4 recording surfaces. Each surface has 1,024 tracks, each track has 64 sectors, and each sector stores 512 bytes. What is its capacity? (Take 1 MB = 2^20 bytes.)
opts: More than one of the above
concept: Disk capacity = number of surfaces × tracks per surface × sectors per track × bytes per sector. Writing each number as a power of 2 makes the multiplication easy: add the powers.
why: A — Correct. 2^27 bytes ÷ 2^20 = 2^7 = 128 MB.
B — Wrong. 64 MB is what you get if you use 2 surfaces instead of 4 (for example, counting platters instead of surfaces).
C — Wrong. 256 MB is what you get if you use 8 surfaces instead of 4.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: How many 700 MB CDs are needed to copy all the data on a full 4.7 GB DVD?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 4.7 GB ÷ 700 MB is about 6.7 to 6.9, so 6 CDs are not enough and 7 are needed.
concept: When a file set must be split across discs, divide the total size by the capacity of one disc and round UP, because a part-filled disc is still needed. Here the answer is the same whether 1 GB is taken as 1,000 MB or as 1,024 MB.
why: A — Wrong. 6 CDs hold only 6 × 700 = 4,200 MB, which is less than 4.7 GB.
B — Correct. 7 CDs hold 4,900 MB, which is enough for 4.7 GB.
C — Wrong. 8 CDs are more than needed, since 7 CDs already hold 4,900 MB.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question, so more than one of A–C cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: Taking 1 GB = 1,000 MB: 4,700 ÷ 700 ≈ 6.71. Taking 1 GB = 1,024 MB: 4,812.8 ÷ 700 ≈ 6.88. In both cases 6 CDs (4,200 MB) are too few and 7 CDs (4,900 MB) are enough, so 7 CDs are needed.
tip: When splitting data across discs, always round UP: 6.7 discs means 7 discs.

q: Which of the following are parts or terms related to a hard disk drive?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Platters, read/write heads, and tracks and sectors are all hard-disk terms, so more than one option is true.
concept: A hard disk has one or more rigid platters coated with magnetic material, spinning at speeds such as 5,400 or 7,200 rpm. Read/write heads on an arm move over the surfaces. Each surface is divided into concentric tracks, and each track into sectors. Tracks at the same position on all surfaces form a cylinder. Access time = seek time (moving the head to the track) + rotational latency (waiting for the sector) + transfer time.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Platters are the spinning magnetic disks inside a hard disk.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Read/write heads read and write the magnetic data on the platters.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each platter surface is divided into tracks, and each track into sectors.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all hard-disk terms, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: How many bits make up one nibble?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A nibble is half a byte, so it has 4 bits.
concept: The bit (0 or 1) is the smallest unit of data. Four bits make a nibble and eight bits make a byte, so a nibble is half a byte. One hexadecimal digit fits exactly in one nibble.
why: A — Correct. A nibble is 4 bits, which is half of a byte.
B — Wrong. 8 bits make one byte, not a nibble.
C — Wrong. 16 bits are two bytes; that is four nibbles, not one.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Taking 1 KB = 1024 bytes (binary convention), which of the following is equal to 1 GB?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In the binary convention 1 GB = 1024 MB = 1024 × 1024 KB = 2^30 bytes, so all three options are equal to 1 GB.
concept: In the binary convention each step up (byte → KB → MB → GB → TB) multiplies by 1024, which is 2^10. So 1 KB = 2^10 bytes, 1 MB = 2^20 bytes, 1 GB = 2^30 bytes and 1 TB = 2^40 bytes. The IEC names for these exact binary sizes are KiB, MiB, GiB and TiB; disk makers often use steps of 1000 instead.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. By definition, 1 GB = 1024 MB in the binary convention.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 1 GB = 1024 MB = 1024 × 1024 KB = 1,048,576 KB.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 1 GB = 1024 × 1024 × 1024 bytes = 2^10 × 2^10 × 2^10 = 2^30 bytes.
D — Correct. All three options are equal to 1 GB.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Remember the powers of 2: KB = 2^10, MB = 2^20, GB = 2^30, TB = 2^40 bytes.

q: How many bits are there in 2 KB? (Take 1 KB = 1024 bytes.)
opts: More than one of the above
concept: To change a bigger unit into bits, first change it into bytes and then multiply by 8, because 1 byte = 8 bits. In the binary convention 1 KB = 1024 bytes. Always check which convention (1024 or 1000) the question gives.
why: A — Wrong. 2,048 is the number of bytes in 2 KB; the question asks for bits, so you must still multiply by 8.
B — Wrong. 16,000 uses 1 KB = 1000 bytes, but the question fixes 1 KB = 1024 bytes.
C — Correct. 2 × 1024 × 8 = 16,384 bits.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: 2 KB = 2 × 1024 bytes = 2048 bytes. 2048 bytes × 8 bits per byte = 16,384 bits.

q: In increasing order of size, which unit comes immediately after the petabyte (PB)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The order is … TB, PB, EB, ZB, YB, so the exabyte comes right after the petabyte.
concept: The units in increasing order are: bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB, EB, ZB, YB. Each unit is 1024 times the one before it in the binary convention (1000 times in the SI convention). So 1 EB = 1024 PB.
why: A — Wrong. The zettabyte comes after the exabyte (1 ZB = 1024 EB), so it is two steps above the petabyte.
B — Wrong. The yottabyte comes after the zettabyte, so it is three steps above the petabyte.
C — Correct. 1 EB = 1024 PB, so the exabyte is the next unit after the petabyte.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Order to remember: K, M, G, T, P, E, Z, Y; the official prefixes added in 2022 after yotta are ronna (R) and quetta (Q).

q: Which of the following storage unit names is NOT defined by any official standard (SI or IEC)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Yotta is an official SI prefix, but 'bronto' and 'geop' are not; brontobyte and geopbyte are only informal names, so two options fit the stem.
concept: The official SI prefixes go kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta, exa, zetta, yotta, and since 2022 ronna (10^27) and quetta (10^30). Brontobyte and geopbyte appear in many exam lists, but they are informal names, not part of any standard. In those informal lists 1 brontobyte = 1024 yottabytes and 1 geopbyte = 1024 brontobytes.
why: A — Wrong. Yotta is an official SI prefix (10^24, added in 1991), so the yottabyte is a standard unit and does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 'Bronto' is not an SI or IEC prefix; brontobyte is only an informal name.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 'Geop' is not an SI or IEC prefix either; geopbyte is also only an informal name.
D — Correct. Both brontobyte and geopbyte are unofficial names, so B and C both fit the stem.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: the notes write '1 Geopbyte = 1 Brontobyte'. In the usual informal list, 1 geopbyte = 1024 brontobytes. The official prefixes after yotta are ronna and quetta (2022).

q: Taking 1 MB = 1024 KB and 1 KB = 1024 bytes, how many bytes are there in 1.5 MB?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: To go down from MB to bytes, multiply by 1024 twice (MB → KB → bytes). To go up, divide by 1024 at each step. Keep to the convention given in the question.
why: B — Wrong. 1,536 is the number of KB in 1.5 MB; one more multiplication by 1024 is needed to reach bytes.
C — Wrong. 1,500,000 uses steps of 1000, but the question fixes steps of 1024.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A pen drive has 16 GB of free space. How many photos of 4 MB each can it store at most? (Take 1 GB = 1024 MB.)
opts: More than one of the above
concept: To find how many files fit, bring both sizes to the same unit and then divide. Here GB is changed to MB (× 1024) and the total is divided by the size of one photo. Real devices fit slightly fewer because the file system also needs some space.
why: A — Wrong. 4,000 comes from 1 GB = 1000 MB, but the question says 1 GB = 1024 MB.
B — Correct. 16 × 1024 ÷ 4 = 4,096 photos.
C — Wrong. 65,536 comes from multiplying by 4 instead of dividing by 4.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: Free space = 16 GB = 16 × 1024 MB = 16,384 MB. Number of photos = 16,384 MB ÷ 4 MB = 4,096.

q: A single binary digit, which can be either 0 or 1, is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A single binary digit is a bit (short for 'binary digit'), which is not among A–C.
concept: Bit = binary digit, the smallest unit of data. 4 bits make a nibble and 8 bits make a byte. A 'word' is the group of bits a CPU handles at one time (for example 32 or 64 bits); its size depends on the processor.
why: A — Wrong. A byte is a group of 8 bits, not one binary digit.
B — Wrong. A nibble is a group of 4 bits.
C — Wrong. A word is a group of bits (such as 32 or 64) that the CPU handles at once.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The correct term is 'bit', which is not listed.

q: Consider the following statements: I. 1 byte = 8 bits. II. 1 nibble = 4 bits. III. In the binary convention, 1 MB = 1024 KB. Which of these is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three statements are true, but every option says 'only' and leaves out a true statement, so the answer is E.
concept: Basic memory units: 1 nibble = 4 bits, 1 byte = 8 bits, and in the binary convention 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB. In statement questions the word 'only' means the other statements are false.
why: A — Wrong. I is correct, but II and III are also correct, so 'I only' is incomplete.
B — Wrong. III is also correct, so 'I and II only' leaves out a true statement.
C — Wrong. I is also correct, so 'II and III only' leaves out a true statement.

D — Wrong. Here 'More than one of the above' means more than one of the options A–C, not more than one of the statements I–III. None of A–C is correct, because each wrongly says 'only', so D cannot apply.
E — Correct. All three statements are true and no option says 'I, II and III', so none of A–C is right.
tip: In statement questions read 'only' carefully: if all statements are true and no option lists all of them, the answer is E. D 'More than one of the above' refers to the options A–C, not to the statements I–III.

q: A hard disk is sold as '500 GB', where the maker uses 1 GB = 10^9 bytes. The operating system shows the size in GiB, where 1 GiB = 2^30 bytes. About how much will it show?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 500 × 10^9 bytes ÷ 2^30 bytes per GiB ≈ 465.7 GiB.
concept: Disk makers use SI (decimal) units: 1 kB = 1000 bytes and 1 GB = 10^9 bytes. Many operating systems count in binary units (1 GiB = 2^30 bytes) but often still label them 'GB'. This is why a new '500 GB' disk seems to have only about 465 GB.
why: B — Wrong. 488.3 comes from 500 × 1000 ÷ 1024, which allows for the 1000-versus-1024 difference at only one of the three steps (bytes → KB → MB → GB); all three steps must be converted.
C — Wrong. A GB (10^9 bytes) is smaller than a GiB (2^30 bytes), so the number cannot stay at 500.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Exam books usually take 1 KB = 1024 bytes unless the question says otherwise.

q: Which device reads the special magnetic-ink characters printed at the bottom of bank cheques?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) reads the magnetic-ink characters on cheques.
concept: MICR reads characters printed with ink that contains iron oxide. Banks use it to read the cheque number, MICR code and other details quickly and with very few errors. In India these characters use the E-13B font.
why: A — Wrong. OMR (Optical Mark Reader) senses marks such as filled bubbles on answer sheets; it does not read magnetic ink.
B — Correct. MICR reads the magnetic-ink characters printed on cheques.
C — Wrong. OCR (Optical Character Recognition) reads ordinary printed text from an image; it is not the standard cheque-reading method.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: MICR → cheques (magnetic ink); OMR → answer sheets (marks); OCR → printed text (characters).

q: Which type of scanner has a flat glass plate on which the page is placed face down while the scanning head moves underneath it?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A flatbed scanner has a flat glass plate and a moving scan head under it.
concept: Scanners are input devices that turn a paper image into digital form. A flatbed scanner (common in offices and photocopiers) has a glass plate and a moving scan head. A handheld scanner is moved by hand over the page. A drum scanner wraps the original around a rotating cylinder and is used for very high-quality professional work.
why: A — Wrong. A handheld scanner is dragged over the page by the user; there is no glass plate to place the page on.
B — Wrong. A drum scanner fixes the original on a rotating drum (cylinder), not on a flat glass plate.
C — Correct. The flatbed scanner is the one with the flat glass plate.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which technology converts a scanned image of printed text into editable and searchable text?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: OCR (Optical Character Recognition) recognises the letters in an image and turns them into text.
concept: OCR = Optical Character Recognition. A scanner or camera first takes a picture of the page; OCR software then recognises each character and saves it as text that can be edited and searched. It is used to digitise books, read vehicle number plates and scan documents with phones.
why: A — Correct. OCR turns an image of printed text into editable text.
B — Wrong. MICR reads only special magnetic-ink characters, such as those on cheques.
C — Wrong. OMR only detects whether marks are present in fixed positions, such as answer bubbles; it does not recognise letters.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: OCR gives editable text; a plain scan without OCR is only a picture of the page.

q: Which of the following is NOT a biometric method of identifying a person?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A password is something the person knows, not a body feature, so it is not biometric.
concept: Biometrics identifies a person from body features or behaviour: fingerprint, face, iris, retina, palm, voice. A password is 'something you know', not a body feature. Aadhaar, for example, records fingerprints, iris scans and a face photograph as biometric data.
why: A — Wrong. A fingerprint is a body feature, so it is biometric and does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. The pattern of the iris in the eye is a biometric feature.
C — Correct. A typed password is knowledge, not a body feature, so it is not biometric.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A light pen is an input device mainly used to
opts: select or draw items directly on the display screen
print pictures using a beam of light
More than one of the above
exp: A light pen is pointed at the screen to select items or draw on it.
concept: A light pen is a pen-shaped pointing device with a light sensor in its tip. When it is touched to the screen, the computer works out where it is pointing, so the user can select menu items or draw. It was used mainly with CRT monitors; today a stylus on a touch screen does a similar job.
why: A — Correct. A light pen lets the user point, select and draw directly on the screen.
B — Wrong. Printing with light (a laser) is done by a laser printer, which is an output device.
C — Wrong. Barcodes are read by a barcode reader.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A digitizer (graphics tablet) is most useful for
opts: reading filled bubbles on answer sheets
turning drawings and maps into digital form by tracing them with a stylus
More than one of the above
exp: A digitizer senses the position of a stylus on its flat surface and sends it to the computer, so drawings and maps can be traced into digital form.
concept: A digitizer, or graphics tablet, is an input device with a flat surface and a stylus (or a puck). The tablet senses where the stylus is and sends these coordinates to the computer. Architects, engineers and artists use it for CAD, maps and digital drawing.
why: A — Wrong. Reading bubbles on answer sheets is the job of an OMR.
B — Correct. Tracing drawings and maps with a stylus is the main use of a digitizer.
C — Wrong. Printing large drawings is done by a plotter, which is an output device.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A barcode reader reads the code on a product label by
opts: detecting magnetic ink in the bars
sensing the pressure of the label
measuring the light reflected from the dark bars and light spaces
More than one of the above
exp: A barcode reader shines light on the code; dark bars reflect little light and light spaces reflect more, and this pattern is decoded.
concept: A barcode stores data (usually a number) as dark bars and light spaces of different widths. The reader uses a laser, LEDs or a small camera; the dark bars reflect little light and the spaces reflect a lot. The reader turns this pattern into the number and sends it to the computer, as at supermarket billing counters.
why: A — Wrong. Magnetic ink is read by MICR (on bank cheques), not by barcode readers.
B — Wrong. Barcode reading is optical; no pressure is involved.
C — Correct. The reader decodes the pattern of reflected light.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Consider the following statements about QR codes: I. A QR code is a two-dimensional (matrix) code. II. A QR code can store more data than a standard one-dimensional barcode. III. A QR code can be read only by a laser scanner, not by a phone camera. Which of these is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because ordinary phone cameras read QR codes every day.
concept: QR stands for Quick Response; the code was developed in 1994 by Denso Wave in Japan. It stores data in a square grid of black and white modules (in two dimensions), so it holds much more data than a 1D barcode, which stores data only across its width. Any smartphone camera with suitable software can read it, which is why UPI payments use QR codes.
why: A — Wrong. I is correct, but II is also correct, so 'I only' is incomplete.
B — Correct. I and II are true; III is false because phone cameras read QR codes (for example for UPI payments).
C — Wrong. III is false, so 'II and III only' cannot be right.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following are input devices?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A scanner, a joystick and a trackball all send data into the computer, so all three are input devices.
concept: Input devices send data or commands into the computer. A scanner inputs images, a joystick inputs direction and button presses (mostly for games and simulators), and a trackball is a pointing device like an upside-down mouse whose ball is rolled by the fingers.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A scanner turns a paper image into digital data for the computer.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A joystick sends direction and button signals to the computer.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A trackball moves the pointer on the screen, like a mouse.
D — Correct. All three are input devices.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT an input device?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A plotter produces drawings on paper, so it is an output device, not an input device.
concept: Ask 'Which way does the data flow?'. Data going into the computer means an input device (keyboard, mouse, microphone, webcam, scanner). Data coming out of the computer to the user means an output device (monitor, printer, plotter, speaker).
why: A — Correct. A plotter prints large drawings on paper, so it is an output device.
B — Wrong. A microphone sends sound into the computer, so it is an input device.
C — Wrong. A webcam sends video into the computer, so it is an input device.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which device reads pencil or pen marks filled in the bubbles of a multiple-choice answer sheet?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Marked bubbles are read by an OMR (Optical Mark Reader), which is not among A–C.
concept: An OMR (Optical Mark Reader / Optical Mark Recognition) shines light on the sheet and detects which fixed positions are dark (marked). It does not read letters; it only checks whether a mark is present. Competitive exams commonly use OMR answer sheets.
why: A — Wrong. MICR reads magnetic-ink characters on cheques.
B — Wrong. OCR recognises printed letters and numbers from an image; filled bubbles are read by OMR.
C — Wrong. A barcode reader reads bar patterns on product labels.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The correct device, OMR, is not among the options.
tip: Do not confuse OMR (marks) with OCR (characters) and MICR (magnetic-ink characters).

q: The MICR code printed on Indian bank cheques has how many digits?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The MICR code on Indian cheques has 9 digits: 3 for the city, 3 for the bank and 3 for the branch.
concept: The MICR code on Indian cheques is a 9-digit number: the first 3 digits are the city code, the next 3 the bank code and the last 3 the branch code. It is printed in magnetic ink so that cheque-sorting machines can read it. Do not confuse it with the IFSC, which has 11 characters.
why: A — Wrong. 6 digits is the length of an Indian PIN code, not of the MICR code.
B — Wrong. 11 characters is the length of the IFSC (Indian Financial System Code), used for online transfers.
C — Correct. The MICR code has 9 digits (city–bank–branch, 3 each).
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: MICR code = 9 digits; IFSC = 11 characters; PIN code = 6 digits.

q: Which of the following is an impact printer?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A dot-matrix printer strikes pins against an inked ribbon, so it is an impact printer.
concept: Impact printers form characters by striking an inked ribbon against the paper: dot-matrix, daisy-wheel and line printers. They are noisy but can print carbon copies. Non-impact printers (laser, inkjet, thermal) print without striking the paper and are quieter, with better quality.
why: A — Wrong. A laser printer uses a laser, a drum and toner powder fused by heat; nothing strikes the paper.
B — Correct. Pins in the print head strike an inked ribbon against the paper.
C — Wrong. An inkjet printer sprays tiny drops of ink onto the paper, so it is non-impact.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Impact = strikes a ribbon (dot-matrix, daisy-wheel, line). Non-impact = laser, inkjet, thermal.

q: A dot-matrix printer prints 200 characters per second (CPS). A page has 50 lines with 80 characters in each line. At this rated speed, how long does it take to print one full page?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: One page has 50 × 80 = 4,000 characters, and 4,000 ÷ 200 CPS = 20 seconds.
concept: Printer speed units: CPS (characters per second) for character printers such as dot-matrix, LPM (lines per minute) for line printers, and PPM (pages per minute) for laser and inkjet printers. Time = amount of work ÷ speed, with both in the same unit.
why: A — Wrong. 0.4 seconds (80 ÷ 200) is the time for one line only; the page has 50 lines.
B — Wrong. 2.5 is 200 ÷ 80, which is the number of lines printed per second, not the time for a page.
C — Correct. 4,000 characters ÷ 200 characters per second = 20 seconds.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: Characters per page = 50 lines × 80 characters = 4,000 characters. Time = 4,000 ÷ 200 CPS = 20 seconds.

q: Which of the following printers is NOT an impact printer?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A thermal printer uses heat on special paper and does not strike the paper, so it is a non-impact printer.
concept: Impact printers strike a ribbon against the paper: dot-matrix, daisy-wheel and line (drum, chain or band) printers. Non-impact printers do not strike the paper: laser, inkjet and thermal printers. A thermal printer uses heat on heat-sensitive paper, as in shop bills and ATM slips.
why: A — Correct. A thermal printer uses heat, not striking, so it is non-impact.
B — Wrong. A daisy-wheel printer strikes a petal carrying a raised character against the ribbon, so it is an impact printer.
C — Wrong. A line printer (drum, chain or band type) hammers characters against a ribbon one line at a time, so it is an impact printer.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The smallest single point of an image that a display screen can show is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The smallest point of a displayed image is a pixel (picture element), which is not among A–C.
concept: A pixel (picture element) is one tiny dot of the screen image. The image is a grid of pixels, and resolution is the number of pixels across and down (for example 1920 × 1080). Dot pitch is the distance between neighbouring dots, and refresh rate is how many times per second the image is redrawn (in Hz).
why: A — Wrong. Dot pitch is the distance between two neighbouring dots on the screen (in mm), not the dot itself.
B — Wrong. Refresh rate is the number of times per second the screen is redrawn, measured in Hz.
C — Wrong. Resolution is the total number of pixels across and down, such as 1920 × 1080.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The correct term, pixel (picture element), is not among the options.

q: A screen of 1024 × 768 pixels uses 24-bit colour (3 bytes per pixel). How much memory is needed to store one full screen image? (Take 1 MB = 2^20 bytes.)
opts: More than one of the above
concept: Image memory = number of pixels × bits per pixel. Divide by 8 to get bytes, then by 1024 for KB and again by 1024 for MB. Colour depth decides how many colours can be shown: n bits per pixel gives 2^n colours, so 24-bit colour gives about 16.7 million colours.
why: A — Wrong. 0.75 MB is the size at 1 byte (8 bits) per pixel; 24-bit colour needs 3 bytes per pixel.
B — Correct. 786,432 pixels × 3 bytes = 2,359,296 bytes = 2.25 MB.
C — Wrong. 18 is the size in megabits (786,432 × 24 bits ÷ 2^20); it was not divided by 8 to change bits into bytes.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The refresh rate of a monitor is measured in
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Refresh rate is the number of times per second the screen is redrawn, so it is measured in hertz (Hz).
concept: Refresh rate is how many times per second the monitor redraws the image. 60 Hz means 60 times a second; gaming monitors use 120–240 Hz for smoother motion. DPI measures the resolution of printers and scanners, and PPM measures the speed of page printers.
why: A — Wrong. DPI measures the resolution of printers and scanners.
B — Wrong. PPM measures the speed of page printers such as laser printers.
C — Correct. Refresh rate is given in hertz, i.e. times per second.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Hz → monitor refresh rate; DPI → printer/scanner resolution; CPS, LPM, PPM → printer speed.

q: Consider the following statements about displays: I. A CRT monitor uses an electron beam that strikes a phosphor-coated screen. II. A typical 'LED monitor' is an LCD panel lit by an LED backlight.
