III. In an OLED screen each pixel gives out its own light, so no backlight is needed. Which of these is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three statements are true.
concept: A CRT (cathode ray tube) monitor fires electron beams at phosphor dots that glow. The liquid crystals in an LCD do not make light, so they need a backlight; older LCDs used CCFL tubes and most now use LEDs, which is why they are sold as 'LED monitors'. OLED (organic LED) pixels give out their own light, which allows true black and very thin screens.
why: A — Correct. All three statements are true.
B — Wrong. III is also true, so 'I and II only' leaves out a correct statement.
C — Wrong. II is also true, so 'I and III only' leaves out a correct statement.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: an 'LED monitor' is usually an LCD with LED backlighting; its pixels are not LEDs. OLED is the type whose pixels give out light.

q: A plotter is an output device mainly used to produce
opts: large, precise drawings such as engineering designs, maps and building plans
More than one of the above
exp: A plotter draws large, precise drawings such as CAD designs, maps and building plans.
concept: A plotter draws on large sheets of paper using pens (pen plotter) or ink jets (wide-format plotter). It is used for CAD drawings, maps, building plans and banners. It is an output device because it produces hard copy from the computer.
why: A — Wrong. Small shop bills are usually printed by thermal or dot-matrix receipt printers.
B — Correct. Large, precise drawings are the main use of a plotter.
C — Wrong. Sound output comes from speakers or headphones.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following units are used to express the speed of printers?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: CPS, LPM and PPM are all printer-speed units, used for different kinds of printers.
concept: Printer speed is measured according to how the printer works. Character printers such as dot-matrix are rated in CPS, line printers in LPM, and page printers such as laser and inkjet printers in PPM. Print quality is measured separately in DPI (dots per inch).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. CPS is used for character (serial) printers such as dot-matrix printers.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. LPM is used for line printers, which print a whole line at a time.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. PPM is used for page printers such as laser and inkjet printers.
D — Correct. All three are units of printer speed.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: DPI measures print quality (resolution), not speed.

q: Output printed on paper is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Printed output on paper is hard copy.
concept: Hard copy is permanent output on paper (or another physical medium) from printers and plotters. Soft copy is output shown on a screen or kept as a file, which can be changed easily. A monitor gives soft copy; a printer gives hard copy.
why: A — Wrong. Soft copy is output seen on a screen or kept as a file, not printed on paper.
B — Wrong. A backup copy is an extra copy of data kept for safety; the term says nothing about paper.
C — Correct. Output printed on paper is called hard copy.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Soft copy = on screen or in a file; hard copy = on paper.

q: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: PS/2 ports connect a keyboard and a mouse; the RJ-11 and RJ-45 uses are swapped in A and B.
concept: RJ-45 is the 8-pin connector on Ethernet (LAN) cables. RJ-11 is the smaller connector used for telephone lines and DSL modems. PS/2 is a round 6-pin mini-DIN port for a keyboard or mouse (purple for keyboard, green for mouse), now largely replaced by USB.
why: A — Wrong. RJ-11 is used for telephone lines; Ethernet cables use RJ-45.
B — Wrong. RJ-45 is used for Ethernet; telephone lines use RJ-11.
C — Correct. PS/2 ports are for a keyboard and a mouse.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which connector carries both high-definition digital video and digital audio on a single cable?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface) carries digital video and audio together on one cable.
concept: HDMI sends digital video and audio together, so one cable can connect a laptop or set-top box to a TV. VGA (Video Graphics Array) is an older 15-pin connector that carries only analog video. DisplayPort is another interface that carries digital video and audio.
why: A — Wrong. VGA carries only analog video; sound needs a separate cable.
B — Correct. HDMI carries digital video and audio on one cable.
C — Wrong. PS/2 connects a keyboard or a mouse; it carries no video or audio.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: VGA = analog video only; HDMI = digital video and audio together.

q: Which of the following can work as both input and output devices?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A touch screen, a modem and a headset with a microphone all send data into and receive data from the computer.
concept: Some devices both send data into the computer and receive data from it. A touch screen displays output and accepts touch input. A modem sends and receives data over a line. A headset with a built-in microphone plays sound out (earphones) and takes voice in (microphone). Plain headphones without a microphone are only output devices.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A touch screen shows output and takes touch input.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A modem both sends and receives data.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Its earphones give output and its microphone takes input.
D — Correct. All three work as both input and output devices.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: the notes list 'headphone' as both input and output. Headphones alone are output; only a headset with a microphone is both.

q: Which of the following is NOT a toggle key on a standard PC keyboard?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Shift works only while it is held down, so it is a modifier key, not a toggle key.
concept: A toggle key switches a mode on or off each time it is pressed, and often has an indicator light: Caps Lock, Num Lock and Scroll Lock. Shift, Ctrl and Alt are modifier keys: they change other keys only while they are held down.
why: A — Correct. Shift is a modifier key that acts only while held down; it is not a toggle key.
B — Wrong. Caps Lock turns capital letters on and off with each press, so it is a toggle key.
C — Wrong. Num Lock turns the numeric keypad on and off, so it is a toggle key.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Toggle keys are the three 'Lock' keys: Caps Lock, Num Lock and Scroll Lock.

q: The standard keyboard layout is called QWERTY because
opts: it is named after its inventor
these are the first six letters on the top row of letter keys
it is a short form of 'Quick Writing Electronic Typewriter'
More than one of the above
exp: Q, W, E, R, T and Y are the first six letters on the top letter row of the keyboard.
concept: The QWERTY layout comes from typewriters designed by Christopher Latham Sholes in the 1870s. Its name is simply the first six letters, Q-W-E-R-T-Y, on the top letter row. Other layouts include Dvorak and AZERTY (used in France).
why: A — Wrong. The layout was designed by Christopher Latham Sholes; 'QWERTY' is not anyone's name.
B — Correct. The name comes from the first six letters on the top letter row.
C — Wrong. QWERTY is not an abbreviation; it just lists the first six keys.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: USB stands for
opts: More than one of the above
exp: USB stands for Universal Serial Bus, which is not among A–C.
concept: USB = Universal Serial Bus. It sends data one bit after another (serially) and can also supply power to devices. It replaced older serial, parallel and PS/2 ports. Common connectors are Type-A and Type-C.
why: A — Wrong. The 'S' stands for Serial, not System.
B — Wrong. The 'U' stands for Universal, not Unified.
C — Wrong. The 'S' stands for Serial, not Synchronous.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The correct full form, Universal Serial Bus, is not listed.
tip: USB is a serial bus: data travels one bit after another.

q: Which of the following is system software?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: An operating system manages the hardware and runs other programs, so it is system software.
concept: System software manages the computer hardware and provides a platform for other programs; examples are operating systems and device drivers. Application software does particular jobs for the user, such as writing documents or playing videos.
why: A — Wrong. Word is application software for writing documents.
B — Wrong. VLC is application software for playing audio and video.
C — Correct. The operating system is the main system software.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Programs such as disk clean-up, disk defragmenter and backup tools, which help to maintain and optimise a computer, are called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Tools that maintain and optimise the computer are utility software.
concept: Utility software (system utilities) helps to manage, maintain and protect a computer: disk clean-up, defragmenter, backup, file-compression and antivirus programs. Many books, including NCERT, treat utilities as part of system software, because they support the computer rather than the user's own tasks.
why: A — Wrong. Application software is made for the user's tasks such as writing or browsing, not for maintaining the computer.
B — Correct. These maintenance tools are utility software.
C — Wrong. Firmware is software stored permanently in a hardware chip (such as the BIOS); disk clean-up tools are ordinary programs on the disk.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A device driver, such as a printer driver, belongs to which category of software?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A device driver lets the operating system control a hardware device, so it is system software.
concept: A device driver lets the operating system talk to a particular hardware device (printer, graphics card, Wi-Fi adapter). It works closely with the OS and the hardware, so it is system software. Without the right driver, the OS cannot use the device properly.
why: A — Correct. Device drivers are system software.
B — Wrong. Application software serves the user's own tasks; a driver serves the OS and the hardware.
C — Wrong. Middleware connects different applications or services; a driver connects the OS to a hardware device.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: the notes also list device drivers under 'utilities'. They are system software.

q: Firmware is best described as
opts: a hardware part made of hard plastic
software stored permanently in a hardware chip (ROM or flash), such as the BIOS
an app downloaded from an app store to edit photos
More than one of the above
exp: Firmware is software kept in non-volatile memory (ROM or flash) inside a device, such as a PC's BIOS.
concept: Firmware is low-level software kept in non-volatile memory (ROM or flash) on a device. It controls the device directly and starts working as soon as the power is on. Examples: the BIOS/UEFI of a PC and the software inside routers, washing machines and keyboards. It can often be updated (a 'firmware update').
why: A — Wrong. Firmware is software, not a physical part.
B — Correct. Firmware is software stored permanently in a chip, such as the BIOS.
C — Wrong. A photo-editing app is application software stored on the normal disk.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is an example of Software as a Service (SaaS)?
opts: Google Docs used through a web browser
More than one of the above
exp: Google Docs is ready-to-use software delivered over the internet, so it is SaaS.
concept: Cloud services have three main models. SaaS gives ready-to-use software over the internet (Google Docs, Gmail, Microsoft 365, Zoom). PaaS gives a platform on which you build and run your own apps (Heroku, Google App Engine). IaaS gives basic computing resources such as virtual machines and storage (Amazon EC2).
why: A — Wrong. Amazon EC2 rents out virtual machines, which is IaaS.
B — Wrong. Heroku gives a platform to deploy your own apps, which is PaaS.
C — Correct. Google Docs is finished software used through the browser, which is SaaS.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: SaaS = use ready software; PaaS = build your app on a platform; IaaS = rent servers and storage.

q: In which cloud model does the provider rent out virtual machines, storage and networking, while the customer installs and manages its own operating system and applications?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: When the provider gives only the infrastructure and the customer manages the OS and apps, the model is IaaS.
concept: Think of the cloud models as layers. In IaaS the provider gives the infrastructure (virtual machines, storage, network) and you manage the OS, runtime and apps. In PaaS the provider also manages the OS and runtime, and you bring only your code. In SaaS the provider manages everything and you just use the software.
why: A — Correct. The provider supplies only the infrastructure and the customer manages the rest, which is IaaS.
B — Wrong. In PaaS the provider manages the OS and runtime; the customer only deploys code.
C — Wrong. In SaaS the customer simply uses finished software and manages nothing underneath.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Unwanted programs that come pre-installed by the maker on a new phone or laptop, using up space and resources, are called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Unwanted pre-installed software that wastes space and resources is called bloatware.
concept: Bloatware means pre-installed or unnecessary software that takes storage, memory or battery but gives the user little value, such as trial antivirus versions and promotional games. It is usually not harmful like malware, but it can slow a device down. Users can often uninstall or disable it.
why: A — Wrong. Firmware is essential low-level software inside hardware, not unwanted extras.
B — Wrong. Middleware connects applications so they can exchange data.
C — Correct. Unwanted pre-installed software of this kind is called bloatware.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Software that sits between different applications (or between applications and databases or the operating system) and helps them communicate and exchange data is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Software that connects applications so they can talk to each other is called middleware.
concept: Middleware is 'software glue'. It lets separate programs, often running on different computers, talk to each other and share data. Examples include message brokers (such as Apache Kafka), database connectivity layers (such as ODBC and JDBC) and application servers.
why: A — Wrong. Freeware is a licence type (free to use); it says nothing about connecting applications.
B — Correct. Middleware connects applications so they can communicate.
C — Wrong. Shareware is a licence type (try before you buy), not connecting software.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT application software?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The BIOS is firmware that starts the computer, so it is not application software.
concept: Application software helps users do particular jobs: spreadsheets, media players, browsers, games. The BIOS is firmware stored on the motherboard; it tests the hardware at start-up and begins loading the operating system, so it is system-level software.
why: A — Correct. The BIOS is firmware (system-level software), not application software.
B — Wrong. Excel is a spreadsheet application, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. VLC is a media-player application, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Consider the following statements: I. System software manages the hardware and provides a platform for other programs. II. Application software is made to do specific tasks for the user, such as word processing. III. Application software normally controls the hardware directly, without any system software. Which of these is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because applications use the hardware through the operating system and drivers.
concept: System software (operating system, device drivers, utilities) works close to the hardware. Application software runs on top of the operating system and asks it to use the hardware on its behalf. Users mostly work with application software, while system software runs in the background.
why: A — Wrong. II is also correct, so 'I only' is incomplete.
B — Correct. I and II are true; III is false.
C — Wrong. III is false, because applications reach the hardware through system software.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following are examples of system software?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The operating system and device drivers are system software; a spreadsheet program is application software. Two options are true, so the answer is D.
concept: System software includes operating systems, device drivers, utility programs and, in many books, language translators. Application software includes word processors, spreadsheets, browsers, media players and games.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The operating system is the main system software.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A device driver lets the operating system control a hardware device.
C — Wrong. A spreadsheet program such as Excel is application software.
D — Correct. A and B are both system software.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is utility software?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: None of the three is a utility: PowerPoint and Chrome are applications and the kernel is the core of an operating system.
concept: Utility software maintains, protects or optimises the computer: antivirus, disk clean-up, disk defragmenter, backup and file-compression tools. A presentation program and a web browser are application software, and a kernel is the core of an operating system.
why: A — Wrong. PowerPoint is application software for presentations.
B — Wrong. The kernel is the core of the operating system, not a utility.
C — Wrong. Chrome is application software for browsing the web.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. None of the three is a utility; examples of utilities are antivirus and disk defragmenter programs.

q: Shareware is software that
opts: can be tried free for a limited time or with limited features, after which the user is expected to pay
has no copyright, so anyone may do anything with it
must always come with its source code
More than one of the above
exp: Shareware follows 'try before you buy': a free trial, then payment for continued or full use.
concept: Shareware follows 'try before you buy'. Users may try and share the trial copy, but for long-term or full use they are expected to buy a licence. WinRAR and WinZip are well-known examples. Shareware is usually closed source.
why: A — Correct. This is the 'try before you buy' model of shareware.
B — Wrong. Software with no copyright is public-domain software.
C — Wrong. Giving the source code is a feature of open-source software; shareware usually does not include it.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Shareware = try first, pay later; freeware = free but closed; open source = source shared under a licence.

q: Consider the following statements: I. Open-source software has no licence at all. II. GPL and MIT are open-source licences. III. Open-source software may be sold for money. Which of these is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: II and III are true; I is false because open-source software is always released under a licence.
concept: Open-source software is copyrighted and released under a licence that lets anyone view, change and share the source code. Common licences are the GPL (copyleft) and permissive licences such as MIT, Apache and BSD. These licences allow selling copies or services; 'free' here means freedom, not zero price.
why: A — Wrong. I is false: open-source software always has a licence.
B — Wrong. I is false, so any option containing I is wrong.
C — Correct. II and III are true; I is false because open-source software is always licensed.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: the notes call open source 'licence-free'. It IS licensed; the licence is what gives users their freedoms.

q: Who started the GNU Project and founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Richard Stallman announced the GNU Project in 1983 and founded the FSF in 1985.
concept: Richard Stallman announced the GNU Project in 1983 to build a free Unix-like operating system, and founded the Free Software Foundation in 1985. He also wrote the GNU General Public License (GPL). Linus Torvalds wrote the Linux kernel in 1991, which was combined with GNU tools to make complete GNU/Linux systems.
why: A — Wrong. Linus Torvalds created the Linux kernel (1991), not the GNU Project or the FSF.
B — Correct. Richard Stallman started GNU and founded the FSF.
C — Wrong. Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is a well-known example of public-domain software (no copyright claimed)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SQLite's authors placed its code in the public domain; VLC and GIMP are copyrighted open-source programs.
concept: Public-domain software has no copyright owner, so anyone may use, change or sell it without conditions. The authors of SQLite placed it in the public domain. VLC and GIMP are free and open source, but they are copyrighted and released under licences (GPL/LGPL), so they are not public domain.
why: A — Wrong. VLC is open source under the GPL/LGPL; it is copyrighted, not public domain.
B — Wrong. GIMP is open source under the GPL; it is copyrighted, not public domain.
C — Correct. SQLite is public-domain software.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: the notes list VLC, Audacity, GIMP, Apache, LibreOffice and FileZilla as public domain. They are open source but copyrighted.

q: Which of the following is NOT open-source software?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Windows is proprietary; its source code is not published.
concept: Proprietary (closed-source) software keeps its source code secret, and the owner controls its use through a licence: Windows, MS Office, Adobe Photoshop. Open-source software publishes its source code under a licence: the Linux kernel (GPL), Firefox (Mozilla Public License), LibreOffice.
why: A — Correct. Windows is proprietary software, so it is not open source.
B — Wrong. The Linux kernel is open source under the GPL, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. Firefox is open source under the Mozilla Public License, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Software that is free of cost, but whose source code is usually not given and which users may not modify, is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: This describes freeware, which is not among A–C.
concept: Freeware costs nothing to use, but the owner keeps the copyright and usually keeps the source code closed, so users cannot study or change it. Adobe Acrobat Reader is a common example. 'Free of cost' (freeware) is different from 'free as in freedom' (open source).
why: A — Wrong. Open-source software gives its source code and allows changes.
B — Wrong. Shareware is not free for long-term use; payment is expected after the trial.
C — Wrong. Public-domain software has no copyright, so anyone may change it.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The description is of freeware, which is not listed.
tip: Freeware is 'free of cost', not 'free to modify'.

q: A developer changes a program released under the GNU GPL and distributes the changed version to other people. What does the GPL require?
opts: Nothing, because GPL software is in the public domain
The changed version must also be released under the GPL, with its source code available to those who receive it
The developer must pay a fee to the original author before sharing it
More than one of the above
exp: The GPL is a copyleft licence: a distributed changed version must keep the same licence and give access to its source code.
concept: The GPL is a 'copyleft' licence. Anyone may use, study, change and share GPL software, but whoever distributes a changed version must pass on the same freedoms: the same licence and access to the source code. Permissive licences such as MIT do not have this condition.
why: A — Wrong. GPL software is copyrighted and licensed; it is not in the public domain.
B — Correct. Copyleft requires the changed version to stay under the GPL with its source available.
C — Wrong. The GPL does not require paying the original author; it only requires keeping the same freedoms.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Copyleft is 'share-alike': the freedoms must travel with the software.

q: Which of the following are proprietary (closed-source) software?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Microsoft Office, Adobe Photoshop and macOS are all owned by companies that keep their source code private.
concept: Proprietary software is owned by a company that keeps the source code private and sells or grants licences to use it. Microsoft Office, Adobe Photoshop, Windows and macOS are common examples. Using it without a valid licence is software piracy.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Microsoft Office is sold under Microsoft's licence and its code is closed.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Photoshop is Adobe's closed-source product.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. macOS as a whole is proprietary, even though Apple publishes some of its parts as open source.
D — Correct. All three are proprietary software.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: An assembler is a program that converts
opts: a high-level language into machine code one line at a time
machine code back into a high-level language
More than one of the above
exp: An assembler translates assembly-language mnemonics into binary machine code.
concept: An assembler translates assembly-language mnemonics (such as MOV and ADD) into binary machine code. Compilers and interpreters translate high-level languages. Turning machine code back into a readable form is done by a disassembler (to assembly) or a decompiler (towards a high-level language).
why: A — Correct. This is the job of an assembler.
B — Wrong. Translating a high-level language line by line is the job of an interpreter.
C — Wrong. Going from machine code back towards a high-level language is done by a decompiler, not an assembler.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which translator translates and executes a high-level program one statement at a time?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: An interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time.
concept: An interpreter reads one statement, translates it and runs it, then moves to the next. It does not create a separate object or executable file. Languages such as Python and JavaScript are usually run through interpreters (often helped by JIT compilation).
why: A — Wrong. A compiler translates the whole program first; the result is run afterwards.
B — Correct. An interpreter works one statement at a time.
C — Wrong. An assembler translates assembly language, not a high-level language.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT true about an interpreter?
opts: It translates and runs the program one statement at a time
It stops when it reaches a statement that has an error
It produces a separate object file that can be run later without the interpreter
More than one of the above
exp: An interpreter does not produce an object file; making a separate object file is what a compiler does.
concept: An interpreter works statement by statement and runs each one straight away. When it meets an error it stops there, so errors are found one at a time. It does not save an object or executable file, so the interpreter is needed every time the program runs. A compiler, in contrast, makes an object/executable file that can run on its own.
why: A — Wrong. This is true of an interpreter, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. This is true: the interpreter halts at the first error it reaches.
C — Correct. This is false for an interpreter; producing a separate object file is a feature of a compiler.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which program joins one or more object files with library code to produce a single executable file?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The linker combines object files and library routines into one executable file.
concept: After compilation, each source file becomes an object file. The linker combines these object files with the library routines they need (such as printf in C) and fixes the addresses between them, producing one executable file. The loader then places this file in memory to run it.
why: A — Correct. Joining object files and libraries into an executable is the linker's job.
B — Wrong. A loader places an already-built executable into main memory so it can run.
C — Wrong. A debugger helps find and fix errors, for example by running a program step by step.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: The linker makes the executable file; the loader puts it into RAM to run.

q: Which system program copies an executable program from secondary storage into main memory so that it can be run?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The loader brings an executable program from disk into RAM and starts it.
concept: The loader is part of the operating system. It reads the executable file from the disk, places it in RAM, sets up its memory addresses and passes control to the program's first instruction. In short: the linker builds the executable and the loader runs it.
why: A — Wrong. The linker builds the executable from object files; it does not place the program in memory to run.
B — Correct. The loader copies the program into main memory for execution.
C — Wrong. A text editor is used to write or change source code.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: In a C program, lines beginning with # (such as #include and #define) are handled before compilation by the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The C preprocessor handles #include, #define and other # directives before the compiler starts.
concept: The C preprocessor runs before the compiler. It copies in header files (#include), replaces macros (#define) and handles conditional compilation (#ifdef). The compiler then translates the expanded source code.
why: A — Wrong. The linker works after compilation, joining object files.
B — Wrong. The loader works at run time, placing the program in memory.
C — Correct. # directives are processed by the preprocessor.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler, such as the one in the Java Virtual Machine, works by
opts: translating the whole source program into machine code long before it is ever run
compiling bytecode or frequently used code into native machine code while the program is running
checking only the spelling of comments in the program
More than one of the above
exp: A JIT compiler compiles code into native machine code during execution, just before it is needed.
concept: A JIT compiler mixes interpretation and compilation. The program starts running (for example as Java bytecode), and the parts that are used often are compiled into native machine code during execution, which makes them run faster. JIT compilers are used in the JVM, .NET and modern JavaScript engines.
why: A — Wrong. Translating everything well before running is ordinary ahead-of-time compilation, not JIT.
B — Correct. JIT compiles code into machine code while the program runs.
C — Wrong. No compiler's job is to check spelling in comments; comments are ignored.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Consider the following statements: I. A compiler translates the whole program before it is executed. II. A compiled program usually runs faster than the same program run through an interpreter. III. The compiler must be present every time the compiled program is run. Which of these is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because a compiled program runs without the compiler.
concept: A compiler translates the entire source program into an object/executable file in one go and lists all the errors it finds. After that, the executable runs on its own, without the compiler, and usually runs faster than interpreted code. An interpreter, by contrast, must be present every time the program runs.
why: A — Correct. I and II are true; III is false.
B — Wrong. III is false: once compiled, the executable runs without the compiler.
C — Wrong. II is also true, so 'I only' is incomplete.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A program compiles without any error, but stops while running because it tries to divide a number by zero. This is a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: An error that appears only while the program is running, such as division by zero, is a runtime error.
concept: Errors are of three main types. Syntax errors break the grammar of the language and are caught at compile time. Runtime errors happen while the program runs, such as division by zero or trying to open a missing file. Logical errors let the program run but give wrong output because the logic is wrong.
why: A — Wrong. A syntax error would have been caught during compilation, but this program compiled without errors.
B — Wrong. A logical error gives a wrong answer without stopping the program; here the program stops.
C — Correct. Division by zero during execution is a runtime error.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Syntax error → found at compile time; runtime error → while running; logical error → wrong output.

q: A program runs to the end without any error message but prints a wrong result because the formula used is wrong. This is a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: When a program runs but gives a wrong answer because of wrong logic, it is a logical error.
concept: A logical error is a mistake in the program's logic, such as using + instead of −, or the wrong formula. The compiler cannot detect it because the code is valid. It is found by testing the program with known inputs and checking the outputs.
why: A — Correct. A wrong formula that gives a wrong result is a logical error.
B — Wrong. A syntax error stops compilation, but this program ran to the end.
C — Wrong. A linker error (such as a missing function) stops the executable from being built, but this program ran.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Leaving out a required semicolon at the end of a statement in a C program causes a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A missing semicolon breaks the grammar of C, so it is a syntax error that the compiler reports.
concept: Syntax errors are mistakes in the grammar of a language: missing semicolons, unmatched brackets, misspelt keywords. The compiler (or interpreter) reports them before the program can run. They are the easiest errors to fix because the translator points to them.
why: A — Wrong. A logical error is in the meaning of the code, not its grammar; such a program still compiles.
B — Correct. A missing semicolon is a syntax error.
C — Wrong. A runtime error happens while the program runs; a missing semicolon stops it from compiling at all.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Arrange the steps that turn a C source file into a running program in the correct order: P. Linking  Q. Compiling  R. Loading  S. Preprocessing
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The order is preprocessing, compiling, linking, loading: S → Q → P → R.
concept: Source code (.c) → preprocessor → expanded source → compiler (with assembler) → object code (.o/.obj) → linker → executable (.exe) → loader → running program in memory.
why: A — Wrong. Preprocessing must come before compiling, because the compiler needs the expanded code.
B — Wrong. Loading cannot come before linking; the loader needs the finished executable that the linker makes.
C — Correct. Preprocessing → Compiling → Linking → Loading.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: Step 1: the preprocessor handles #include and #define (S). Step 2: the compiler translates the expanded code into object code (Q). Step 3: the linker joins object files and libraries into an executable (P). Step 4: the loader places the executable in memory to run (R). Order: S → Q → P → R.

q: A program as written by a programmer in a high-level language, before it is translated, is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The program as written by the programmer is the source code, which is not among A–C.
concept: Source code is the human-readable program written by the programmer (for example a .c or .py file). A compiler turns it into object code, and the linker then makes executable code. Machine code is the binary instructions that the CPU runs.
why: A — Wrong. Object code is the output of the compiler, not the original program.
B — Wrong. Machine code is binary that the CPU runs, not what the programmer writes in a high-level language.
C — Wrong. Executable code is the final runnable file made by the linker.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. It is called source code, which is not listed.

q: Which of the following are language translators?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Compilers, interpreters and assemblers all translate a program from the language it is written in into a form the computer can execute, so all three are language translators.
concept: A language translator converts a program from one language into another, usually into machine code. A compiler translates a whole high-level program at once, an interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time, and an assembler translates assembly language into machine code.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A compiler translates a whole high-level program into machine (object) code.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. An interpreter translates and runs a high-level program one statement at a time.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. An assembler translates assembly language into machine code.
D — Correct. All three are language translators.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: In the usual classification, third-generation languages (3GLs) are general-purpose high-level languages such as C and Java, while fourth-generation languages (4GLs) are special-purpose, mostly non-procedural languages such as SQL. In this classification, Python is a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Python is a general-purpose high-level language, so it is a third-generation language.
concept: 1GL = machine language; 2GL = assembly language; 3GL = general-purpose high-level languages (FORTRAN, COBOL, C, C++, Java, Python); 4GL = special-purpose languages closer to human language (SQL, report generators, MATLAB, SAS); 5GL = logic/constraint languages used in AI (Prolog, OPS5, Mercury).
why: A — Wrong. 2GL means assembly language, which uses mnemonics close to the machine.
B — Correct. Python is a general-purpose high-level language, so it is a 3GL.
C — Wrong. 4GLs are special-purpose, mostly non-procedural languages such as SQL.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: the notes (and a few online lists) put Python among 4GLs. In the standard classification Python, like C and Java, is a general-purpose 3GL.

q: SQL is usually classified as a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SQL is a fourth-generation language: the user says what data is wanted, not how to get it.
concept: SQL is a fourth-generation language because the user states WHAT data is wanted (for example SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 90) rather than HOW to find it step by step. Other 4GL examples are report generators, MATLAB and SAS. 3GLs like C need step-by-step procedures.
why: A — Wrong. 3GLs such as C and Java are procedural general-purpose languages; SQL is a non-procedural query language.
B — Correct. SQL is the standard example of a 4GL.
C — Wrong. 5GLs such as Prolog are based on logic and constraints for AI problems.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Prolog, a language used in artificial intelligence, is generally classified as a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Prolog is a logic language and is the standard example of a fifth-generation language.
concept: Fifth-generation languages solve problems from facts, rules and constraints given by the programmer, rather than from a step-by-step algorithm. Prolog (1972), OPS5 and Mercury are standard examples. They are linked with AI and with the 'fifth-generation computer' projects of the 1980s.
why: A — Correct. Prolog is a logic language and the standard example of a 5GL.
B — Wrong. 3GLs like C and Java are procedural; Prolog is a logic language.
C — Wrong. 2GL means assembly language, which uses mnemonics for machine instructions.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: In assembly language, short symbolic codes such as ADD, MOV and JMP that stand for machine instructions are called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The symbolic instruction codes of assembly language are called mnemonics.
concept: Assembly language (2GL) replaces binary opcodes with easy-to-remember symbols called mnemonics: MOV (move), ADD (add), JMP (jump). An assembler turns each mnemonic into its binary opcode. Assembly is still machine dependent, because each CPU family has its own instruction set.
why: A — Wrong. A macro is a name given to a group of instructions that is expanded wherever it is used; ADD is a single instruction code.
B — Wrong. A pointer is a variable that holds a memory address.
C — Correct. ADD, MOV and JMP are mnemonics.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Mnemonic means 'memory aid'; the assembler turns each mnemonic into a binary opcode.

q: Which of the following is NOT a high-level language?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Machine language and assembly language are both low-level languages, so two options fit the NOT stem.
concept: Low-level languages are close to the hardware: machine language (1GL, binary) and assembly language (2GL, mnemonics). High-level languages (3GL and above) use English-like words and are mostly machine independent: COBOL, FORTRAN, C, Java, Python.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Machine language (0s and 1s) is the lowest-level language.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Assembly language is low-level; each instruction maps to one machine instruction.
C — Wrong. COBOL (1959) is a high-level language for business, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
D — Correct. Machine language and assembly language are both not high-level.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Consider the following statements about machine language: I. It consists only of binary digits (0s and 1s). II. A machine-language program needs no translator to run. III. A machine-language program written for one CPU family runs unchanged on any other CPU family. Which of these is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true; III is false because machine language is machine dependent.
concept: Machine language is the only language the CPU understands directly, so it needs no translation and runs fastest. But it is machine dependent: each CPU family (for example x86 and ARM) has its own instruction codes. It is also hard to write and error-prone, which is why assembly and high-level languages were created.
why: A — Correct. I and II are true; III is false.
B — Wrong. III is false; machine code written for one CPU family does not run on another.
C — Wrong. III is false, so 'I and III only' cannot be right.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Arrange the following in order from the first generation to the fourth generation of programming languages: P. SQL  Q. Assembly language  R. Machine language  S. C
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Machine language (1GL) → assembly language (2GL) → C (3GL) → SQL (4GL), i.e. R → Q → S → P.
concept: 1GL is machine language. 2GL is assembly language. 3GL means high-level procedural languages such as C. 4GL means non-procedural, problem-oriented languages such as SQL. Each generation is easier for people to use than the one before.
why: A — Wrong. Assembly language (2GL) must come before C (3GL).
B — Wrong. Machine language (1GL) comes before assembly language (2GL).
C — Correct. Machine (1GL) → Assembly (2GL) → C (3GL) → SQL (4GL).
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is a first-generation language (1GL)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The first-generation language is machine language, which is not among A–C.
concept: The first-generation language is machine language: instructions written directly in binary that the CPU runs without translation. Assembly language is a 2GL, FORTRAN (1957) is an early 3GL, and SQL is a 4GL.
why: A — Wrong. Assembly language uses mnemonics, so it is a 2GL, not a 1GL.
B — Wrong. FORTRAN was one of the first high-level languages, but high-level languages are 3GLs.
C — Wrong. SQL is a non-procedural query language, i.e. a 4GL.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. 1GL is machine language, which is not listed.
tip: Do not be misled by 'FORTRAN was the first high-level language'. The first high-level language is not the same as a first-generation language.

q: Consider the following flowchart symbols and their uses: I. Oval (terminal) – start or stop. II. Parallelogram – input or output. III. Diamond – decision. Which of these is/are correctly matched?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three symbols are correctly matched.
concept: Standard flowchart symbols: an oval (or rounded rectangle) for Start/Stop, a parallelogram for input/output (Read/Print), a rectangle for a process (calculation), a diamond for a decision (Yes/No), arrows for the flow of control, and a small circle as a connector.
why: A — Wrong. III is also correctly matched, so 'I and II only' is incomplete.
B — Correct. All three pairs are correct.
C — Wrong. I is also correctly matched, so 'II and III only' is incomplete.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A flowchart does the following: Start → Read A = 7 and B = 12 → Decision: 'Is A > B?' → if Yes, Print A − B; if No, Print B − A → Stop. What is printed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 7 > 12 is false, so the No branch prints B − A = 12 − 7 = 5.
concept: In a flowchart the diamond tests a condition and the flow follows only one branch, Yes or No. To trace it, put in the values and follow the arrows step by step. This flowchart always prints the positive difference of A and B.
why: A — Wrong. −5 is A − B, which is printed only on the Yes branch; 7 > 12 is false.
B — Wrong. 19 is A + B; no addition is done in this flowchart.
C — Correct. The No branch prints 12 − 7 = 5.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: Read A = 7, B = 12. Test 'Is 7 > 12?' → No. Follow the No branch: Print B − A = 12 − 7 = 5. Then Stop.

q: The property that an algorithm must always end after a finite number of steps is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Finiteness means the algorithm must stop after a finite number of steps.
concept: Standard properties of an algorithm (as listed by Donald Knuth): Finiteness – it must stop after a finite number of steps; Definiteness – each step is clear and unambiguous; Input – zero or more inputs; Output – at least one output; Effectiveness – each step is simple enough to be carried out exactly.
why: A — Correct. Finiteness means the algorithm always ends.
B — Wrong. Definiteness means every step is precisely and clearly defined, not that the algorithm stops.
C — Wrong. Generality means the algorithm should work for a whole class of inputs, not just one case.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT a necessary property of an algorithm?
opts: Each step must be clear and unambiguous
It must stop after a finite number of steps
It must be written in a particular programming language
More than one of the above
exp: An algorithm can be written in plain English, as a flowchart or as pseudocode; it does not need any programming language.
concept: An algorithm is a finite, step-by-step procedure for solving a problem. It can be written in plain English, as a flowchart or as pseudocode, and later coded in any programming language. So an algorithm does not depend on a particular programming language.
why: A — Wrong. Clear steps (definiteness) is a required property, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. Stopping after a finite number of steps (finiteness) is a required property.
C — Correct. An algorithm need not be written in any programming language.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following are true about pseudocode?
opts: It describes an algorithm in simple English-like steps
It does not follow the strict syntax of any one programming language
It cannot be run directly by a computer
More than one of the above
exp: All three statements describe pseudocode correctly.
concept: Pseudocode is an informal way of writing an algorithm using short English-like statements and programming ideas such as IF, WHILE, READ and PRINT. It helps to plan a program before coding and is easy for people to read. Because it has no fixed syntax, no compiler or interpreter can run it directly; it must first be turned into real code.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Pseudocode uses simple English-like steps.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Pseudocode has no fixed syntax of any one programming language.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Pseudocode must be converted into a real programming language before a computer can run it.
D — Correct. All three statements about pseudocode are true.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The core part of an operating system that stays in memory and directly manages the CPU, memory and devices is called the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The kernel is the core of the OS that stays in memory and manages the hardware.
concept: The kernel is the heart of the operating system. It is loaded during booting and stays in main memory. It handles process scheduling, memory management, device control and system calls. The shell is the outer layer that takes user commands and passes them to the kernel.
why: A — Correct. The kernel is the core of the OS that manages the hardware.
B — Wrong. The shell is the user-interface layer that passes commands to the kernel; it does not directly manage the hardware.
C — Wrong. A compiler is a language translator, not part of the OS core.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Kernel = the core inside; shell = the interface outside.

q: The part of an operating system that takes commands from the user and passes them to the kernel is called the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The shell is the interface that takes user commands and passes them to the kernel.
concept: A shell is the interface between the user and the kernel. It can be command-line (bash in Linux, Command Prompt or PowerShell in Windows) or graphical (such as the Windows desktop). The user talks to the shell, and the shell asks the kernel to do the work.
why: A — Wrong. The kernel does the work, but it does not take commands directly from the user.
B — Correct. The shell takes the user's commands and passes them to the kernel.
C — Wrong. The loader places programs into memory to run them.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which type of operating system gives each user or program a small slice of CPU time in turn, so that many users can work interactively at the same time?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A time-sharing OS switches the CPU among users in small time slices so that all can work interactively.
concept: A time-sharing (multitasking) OS switches the CPU rapidly among users or programs, giving each a short time slice (quantum), often using round-robin scheduling. The switching is so fast that every user feels the computer is working only for them. Unix was designed as a time-sharing system.
why: A — Wrong. A batch OS runs jobs one after another without user interaction.
B — Wrong. A real-time OS focuses on meeting strict deadlines, not on sharing time among many interactive users.
C — Correct. This describes a time-sharing OS.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which type of operating system must guarantee a response within a strict time limit, as in a car's airbag controller or a pacemaker?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Guaranteed responses within strict deadlines are the job of a real-time operating system, which is not among A–C.
concept: This is a real-time operating system (RTOS). In a hard real-time system a late response counts as a failure (airbags, pacemakers, missile control). Soft real-time systems, such as video streaming, can accept small delays. Examples of RTOS are VxWorks and FreeRTOS.
why: A — Wrong. A batch OS runs grouped jobs with no time guarantee.
B — Wrong. A time-sharing OS gives quick responses to many users, but it does not guarantee strict deadlines.
C — Wrong. A multiprogramming OS aims to keep the CPU busy, not to meet deadlines.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The answer is a real-time OS, which is not listed.

q: Restarting a computer that is already switched on, for example by choosing Restart, is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Restarting a computer that is already on is warm (soft) booting.
concept: Booting means starting the computer and loading the operating system. Cold (hard) booting starts the computer from power-off by pressing the power button. Warm (soft) booting restarts a computer that is already on, using the Restart option or Ctrl+Alt+Del in older systems.
why: A — Wrong. Cold booting starts a computer that was completely switched off.
B — Correct. Restarting a running computer is warm booting.
C — Wrong. Formatting prepares a disk for storing data (and erases it); it is not restarting.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Cold boot = start from power-off; warm boot = restart while the computer is on.

q: When a computer is switched on, the Power-On Self-Test (POST) is carried out by
opts: the operating system, after the user logs in
an application program such as a word processor
More than one of the above
exp: POST is run by the BIOS/UEFI firmware before the operating system is loaded.
concept: POST is the first thing that runs at power-on. The BIOS/UEFI firmware, stored in ROM/flash on the motherboard, checks basic hardware such as the processor, RAM, keyboard and graphics. If it finds a fault it shows an error or gives beep codes; otherwise it looks for a boot device to load the operating system.
why: A — Wrong. POST runs before the operating system is even loaded.
B — Wrong. Application programs can run only after the operating system has started.
C — Correct. The BIOS/UEFI firmware performs POST.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Arrange the steps of booting a PC in the correct order: P. The operating system kernel is loaded into RAM.  Q. BIOS/UEFI runs the Power-On Self-Test.  R. The bootstrap loader (boot loader) is run from the boot device.  S. Power is switched on.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Power on → POST by BIOS/UEFI → boot loader → kernel loaded: S → Q → R → P.
concept: Booting means loading the operating system into memory. The sequence is: power on → BIOS/UEFI (from ROM/flash) → POST → find the boot device → bootstrap loader (for example GRUB or Windows Boot Manager) → kernel loaded into RAM → operating system ready, login screen.
why: A — Correct. S → Q → R → P is the booting order.
B — Wrong. POST must come before the boot loader; the firmware tests the hardware first and only then reads the boot device.
C — Wrong. Nothing can run before power is switched on, and the kernel is loaded by the boot loader, so P cannot come before R.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: 1. Power is switched on (S). 2. The BIOS/UEFI firmware starts and runs POST (Q). 3. The firmware finds the boot device and runs the bootstrap/boot loader (R). 4. The boot loader loads the OS kernel into RAM (P) and the OS starts. Order: S → Q → R → P.

q: Which of the following is NOT a function of an operating system?
opts: Compiling C programs into machine code
More than one of the above
exp: Compiling programs is the job of a compiler, not of the operating system.
concept: The main functions of an operating system are process management (scheduling the CPU), memory management, file management, device (I/O) management, security and the user interface. Translating source code is the job of a compiler, which is a separate program that runs on top of the OS.
why: A — Wrong. Memory management is a core OS function, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Correct. Compiling is done by a compiler, not by the operating system itself.
C — Wrong. Deciding which process gets the CPU is a core OS function.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: MS-DOS mainly provides which type of user interface?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In MS-DOS the user types text commands at a prompt, so it is a command-line interface.
concept: In a CLI the user types text commands (such as DIR or COPY) at a prompt like C:\>. In a GUI the user works with windows, icons, menus and a pointer (WIMP), as in Windows and macOS. MS-DOS (1981) was a single-user, single-tasking, command-line operating system.
why: A — Correct. MS-DOS is a command-line OS.
B — Wrong. A GUI uses windows, icons and a mouse; early Windows versions ran on top of MS-DOS to add a GUI, but MS-DOS itself is command-line.
C — Wrong. Touch interfaces are used in smartphones and tablets, not in MS-DOS.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT an internal DOS command?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: CHKDSK is an external command stored as a separate program file; CLS and TYPE are internal.
concept: Internal DOS commands are built into COMMAND.COM and stay in memory, so they work without any extra file: DIR, COPY, DEL, REN, CLS, TYPE, MD, CD, RD, DATE, TIME, VER. External commands are separate program files on disk that must be present to run: FORMAT, CHKDSK, XCOPY, DISKCOPY, TREE, ATTRIB.
why: A — Wrong. CLS (clear screen) is an internal command, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Correct. CHKDSK is an external command; it is stored as a separate program file on disk.
C — Wrong. TYPE (display a text file) is an internal command.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Internal = built into COMMAND.COM (DIR, COPY, DEL, CLS, TYPE); external = separate files (FORMAT, CHKDSK, XCOPY, DISKCOPY).

q: Which of the following are external DOS commands (stored as separate program files on disk)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: FORMAT, XCOPY and DISKCOPY are all external commands, each stored as its own program file.
concept: External DOS commands are not built into COMMAND.COM; each is a separate program file that must be on the disk to run. Examples: FORMAT, XCOPY, DISKCOPY, CHKDSK, TREE, ATTRIB. Internal commands such as DIR, COPY, DEL, CLS and TYPE are built in and always available.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. FORMAT is a separate program file, so it is an external command.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. XCOPY is a separate program file, so it is an external command.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. DISKCOPY is a separate program file, so it is an external command.
D — Correct. All three are external DOS commands.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which file system is used by default when Windows 10 or Windows 11 is installed on a hard disk or SSD?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Windows 10/11 is installed on NTFS, which is not among A–C.
concept: Windows NT-based systems (such as Windows XP, 7, 10 and 11) install on NTFS (New Technology File System), which supports large files, permissions, encryption and journaling. FAT32 and exFAT are used mostly on pen drives and memory cards. ext4 is common on Linux; HFS+ and APFS are Apple file systems.
why: A — Wrong. ext4 is the common Linux file system.
B — Wrong. HFS+ was the older file system of Apple's macOS.
C — Wrong. APFS is Apple's current file system for macOS and iOS.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The answer is NTFS, which is not listed.

q: An operating system that keeps several programs in main memory at the same time, so that the CPU can switch to another program whenever one is waiting for input/output, is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Keeping several programs in memory so the CPU is never idle while one waits for I/O is multiprogramming.
concept: In multiprogramming, several jobs sit in memory together. When the running job waits for slow I/O, the CPU is given to another job, so the CPU is rarely idle. Time-sharing builds on this idea by also switching jobs after a fixed time slice, so that users can interact.
why: A — Correct. This describes a multiprogramming OS.
B — Wrong. A distributed OS makes many separate computers work together as one system; the stem describes switching programs on one CPU.
C — Wrong. A single-task OS (like MS-DOS) runs only one program at a time.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT an operating system?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Ubuntu, iOS and Android are all operating systems, so none of A–C fits the stem.
concept: Ubuntu is a Linux-based desktop and server OS, iOS is Apple's iPhone OS, and Android is Google's mobile OS built on the Linux kernel. Things that are NOT operating systems include applications (MS Word), web browsers (the Chrome browser) and database systems (MySQL).
why: A — Wrong. Ubuntu is an operating system (a Linux distribution), so it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. iOS is Apple's operating system for iPhones.
C — Wrong. Android is an operating system for phones and tablets.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. All three are operating systems, so none of them is the answer.

q: Consider the following statements: I. A batch operating system groups similar jobs and runs them without user interaction. II. A distributed operating system manages a group of separate computers so that they appear to users as a single system. III. An embedded operating system is built into a device such as a washing machine, router or car system. Which of these is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three statements are true, but every option says 'only' and leaves one out, so the answer is E.
concept: Batch OS: jobs are collected and run in batches with no interaction (early mainframes). Distributed OS: many networked computers share the work and look like one system. Embedded OS: a small OS inside a dedicated device, often real-time. Network OS: provides file and printer sharing over a network (for example Windows Server).
why: A — Wrong. III is also correct, so 'I and II only' is incomplete.
B — Wrong. I is also correct, so 'II and III only' is incomplete.
C — Wrong. II is also correct, so 'I and III only' is incomplete.

D — Wrong. Here 'More than one of the above' means more than one of the options A–C, not more than one of the statements I–III. None of A–C is correct, because each wrongly says 'only', so D cannot apply.
E — Correct. All three statements are true and no option says 'I, II and III'.
tip: In statement questions, D 'More than one of the above' refers to the options A–C, not to the statements I–III. If all the statements are true and no option lists all of them, the answer is E.

q: The Domain Name System (DNS) is used to
opts: send email from one mail server to another
assign MAC addresses to network cards
translate domain names into IP addresses
More than one of the above
exp: DNS translates names such as www.example.com into IP addresses.
concept: Computers find each other by IP address, but people remember names like www.example.com. DNS works like the internet's phone book: a DNS server looks up the name and returns its IP address. DNS uses port 53.
why: A — Wrong. Sending email between servers is done by SMTP.
B — Wrong. MAC addresses are fixed in network cards by the manufacturer; DNS does not assign them.
C — Correct. DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: DNS: domain name → IP address. (ARP then finds the MAC address for an IP address on a local network.)

q: Consider the following protocol and default port pairs: I. HTTP – 80  II. HTTPS – 443  III. SMTP – 25. Which of these is/are correctly matched?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three pairs are correct, but every option leaves at least one out, so the answer is E.
concept: Common default ports: FTP 20 (data) and 21 (control), SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, HTTP 80, POP3 110, IMAP 143, HTTPS 443. A port number tells the receiving computer which service (program) should get the data.
why: A — Wrong. III (SMTP – 25) is also correct, so 'I and II only' is incomplete.
B — Wrong. I (HTTP – 80) is also correct, so 'II and III only' is incomplete.
C — Wrong. II and III are also correct, so 'I only' is incomplete.

D — Wrong. Here 'More than one of the above' means more than one of the options A–C, not more than one of the statements I–III. None of A–C is correct, because each wrongly says 'only', so D cannot apply.
E — Correct. All three pairs are correct and no option lists all of them.
tip: In statement questions, D 'More than one of the above' refers to the options A–C, not to the statements I–III. If all the statements are true and no option lists all of them, the answer is E.

q: Consider the following statements: I. An IPv4 address is 32 bits long. II. An IPv6 address is 128 bits long. III. A MAC address is 48 bits long. Which of these is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three statements are true: IPv4 is 32-bit, IPv6 is 128-bit and MAC is 48-bit.
concept: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers (for example 192.168.1.1). IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as eight groups of hexadecimal digits separated by colons. A MAC (physical) address is 48 bits, written as six pairs of hex digits (for example 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E), and is fixed in the network card.
why: A — Wrong. III is also correct, so 'I and II only' is incomplete.
B — Correct. All three statements are true.
C — Wrong. I is also correct, so 'II and III only' is incomplete.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses. How many times larger is the IPv6 address space than the IPv4 address space?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 2^128 ÷ 2^32 = 2^96, so IPv6 has 2^96 times as many addresses.
concept: With n bits you can make 2^n different addresses. IPv4 has 2^32 (about 4.3 billion) addresses, which have run short. IPv6 has 2^128 (about 3.4 × 10^38) addresses. Adding bits multiplies the number of addresses; it does not just add to it.
why: A — Wrong. 4 is 128 ÷ 32, the ratio of the address lengths in bits, not of the numbers of addresses.
B — Wrong. 96 is 128 − 32, the number of extra bits; each extra bit doubles the count, so the ratio is 2^96, not 96.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: In the URL https://www.example.com/home.html, the part 'https' is the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 'https' is the protocol (scheme) part of the URL.
concept: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) has parts: the protocol or scheme (https://), the domain name (www.example.com), the path (/home.html) and sometimes a query (?id=123). The protocol tells the browser how to fetch the resource; https means HTTP made secure with encryption (TLS).
why: A — Correct. 'https' (HTTP Secure) is the protocol part of the URL.
B — Wrong. The domain name is www.example.com.
C — Wrong. The path (file name) part is /home.html, not 'https'.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Ravi sends an email with Asha in the To field, Bina in the CC field and Chetan in the BCC field. Which of the following is true?
opts: Asha can see that Chetan also received the email
Bina can see that Asha received the email
Chetan's address is shown to both Asha and Bina
More than one of the above
exp: To and CC addresses are visible to every recipient, so Bina sees Asha's address; BCC addresses are hidden from the others.
concept: To: the main recipients. CC (carbon copy): others who get a copy; every recipient can see the To and CC addresses. BCC (blind carbon copy): hidden recipients; their addresses are not shown to the other recipients. BCC is used to protect privacy when mailing many people.
why: A — Wrong. Chetan is in BCC, so Asha cannot see his address.
B — Correct. The To address (Asha) is visible to the CC recipient (Bina).
C — Wrong. BCC addresses are hidden from the To and CC recipients.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: BCC recipients are hidden from everyone else; To and CC addresses are visible to all recipients.

q: ARPANET, the network that grew into the Internet, stands for
opts: More than one of the above
exp: ARPANET = Advanced Research Projects Agency Network, funded by the US Department of Defense.
concept: ARPANET was funded by ARPA (Advanced Research Projects Agency, set up in 1958) of the US Department of Defense. It went live in 1969, first linking four university and research sites. It was one of the first packet-switching networks, and it switched to TCP/IP on 1 January 1983.
why: A — Correct. ARPANET = Advanced Research Projects Agency Network.
B — Wrong. This is not a real expansion; 'ARPA' stands for the Advanced Research Projects Agency.
C — Wrong. ARPANET was a US defence research network, not a 'regional public access' network.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT a web browser?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Bing is Microsoft's search engine, not a web browser.
concept: A web browser is application software that fetches and displays web pages: Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge, Opera. A search engine is a web service that finds pages for a query: Google Search, Bing, DuckDuckGo. You use a browser to open a search engine.
why: A — Wrong. Safari is Apple's web browser, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. Edge is Microsoft's web browser, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Correct. Bing is a search engine, not a browser.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A company's private network that is also opened, with controlled access, to its suppliers and business partners is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A private network that is partly opened to selected outsiders such as suppliers is an extranet.
