concept: The Internet is the worldwide public network of networks. An intranet is a private network that uses internet technology and is meant only for an organisation's own employees. An extranet is part of an intranet opened in a controlled way to selected outsiders such as suppliers, dealers or customers.
why: A — Correct. This describes an extranet.
B — Wrong. An intranet is only for the organisation's own staff, not for outside partners.
C — Wrong. The Internet is public and open to everyone, not a private network.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
opts: PAN — a network spread across a whole country
LAN — a network within a building or campus
WAN — a network limited to one room
More than one of the above
exp: A LAN covers a room, building or campus; the descriptions in A and C belong to other network types.
concept: Networks by area: PAN (Personal Area Network) – around one person, about 10 m (Bluetooth earbuds, phone). LAN (Local Area Network) – a room, building or campus. MAN (Metropolitan Area Network) – a city. WAN (Wide Area Network) – a country or the whole world; the Internet is the largest WAN.
why: A — Wrong. A PAN covers only the area around one person; a country-wide network is a WAN.
B — Correct. A LAN covers a building or campus.
C — Wrong. A WAN covers very large areas such as countries; a one-room network is a LAN or PAN.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Small text files that a website stores in the user's browser to remember things such as login status and preferences are called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Cookies are small pieces of data a website stores in the browser to remember the user.
concept: Cookies are small pieces of data saved by the browser for a website. Session cookies are deleted when the browser closes; persistent cookies stay until they expire or are deleted. They are used for logins, shopping carts, preferences and tracking for advertising.
why: A — Wrong. A plug-in (or extension) is a small program that adds features to the browser.
B — Wrong. A bookmark is a saved link that the user adds to return to a page.
C — Correct. These small files are called cookies.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following protocols are used in sending or receiving email?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SMTP sends email, and POP3 and IMAP are used to receive it, so all three are email protocols.
concept: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, port 25) sends email from the client to the server and between servers. POP3 (Post Office Protocol 3, port 110) downloads mail to one device and usually removes it from the server. IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol, port 143) keeps mail on the server and keeps it in sync across devices.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. SMTP is used to send email.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. POP3 is used to download (receive) email.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. IMAP is used to read and manage email kept on the server.
D — Correct. All three are email protocols.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Malware that copies itself and spreads across a network on its own, without attaching to a host file and without the user running it, is a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A worm is standalone malware that spreads across networks by itself.
concept: A virus attaches itself to a host file or program and spreads when that file is run or shared. A worm is a standalone program that copies itself across networks by itself, often by using security holes. A Trojan pretends to be useful software and does not copy itself.
why: A — Wrong. A virus needs a host file and usually needs the user to run it.
B — Correct. A worm spreads on its own without a host file.
C — Wrong. A Trojan does not copy itself; it tricks the user into installing it.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Virus needs a host file; worm spreads by itself; Trojan pretends to be useful and does not copy itself.

q: Which of the following is NOT a type of malware (malicious software)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Phishing and DoS are attack methods, not kinds of software, so two options fit the NOT stem.
concept: Malware is software: viruses, worms, Trojans, ransomware, spyware, adware and rootkits. Phishing, spam, DoS/DDoS and man-in-the-middle are methods of attack. Attackers may use malware in them (for example a botnet for a DDoS attack), but the attack itself is not a kind of malicious software.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Phishing is a trick (fake emails or websites) to steal details; it is an attack method, not software.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A DoS attack floods a server so that it becomes unavailable; it is an attack, not a type of malware.
C — Wrong. Ransomware is malware that encrypts files and demands payment, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
D — Correct. Phishing and DoS are attacks, not malware.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Common mistake: the notes list spamming, phishing, DoS and MitM under 'types of malware'. They are attacks.

q: Malicious software that pretends to be a useful or harmless program, but secretly harms the system or opens a backdoor for an attacker, is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Malware disguised as a useful program is a Trojan horse.
concept: A Trojan horse is named after the wooden horse of the Greek story: it looks like a gift but hides attackers inside. It does not copy itself; the user is tricked into installing it (for example a fake game or 'free' cracked software). Once inside, it may steal data or let the attacker control the computer.
why: A — Correct. This describes a Trojan horse.
B — Wrong. A worm spreads by itself across networks; it does not depend on pretending to be useful.
C — Wrong. A cookie is a small data file from a website, not a program.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Malware that encrypts the victim's files and demands payment to unlock them is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Ransomware locks or encrypts data and demands a ransom.
concept: Ransomware locks or encrypts data and demands a ransom, often in cryptocurrency. WannaCry (2017) spread worldwide and hit hospitals and companies. Regular offline backups and timely software updates are the best defence.
why: A — Wrong. Adware shows unwanted advertisements.
B — Wrong. Spyware secretly watches the user and steals information; it does not normally lock files for ransom.
C — Correct. Malware that encrypts files for a ransom is ransomware.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is an example of two-factor authentication (2FA)?
opts: Entering a password and then an OTP sent to the registered mobile phone
Using a longer password with symbols and numbers
More than one of the above
exp: A password (something you know) plus an OTP on your phone (something you have) uses two different factors.
concept: Authentication factors are of three kinds: something you know (password, PIN), something you have (phone, OTP token, card) and something you are (fingerprint, face). Two-factor authentication needs two different kinds, such as password + OTP, or card + PIN at an ATM.
why: A — Wrong. Typing the same password twice is still only one factor (something you know).
B — Correct. Password (know) + OTP on the phone (have) are two different factors.
C — Wrong. A stronger password is still only one factor.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Arrange the following malware in chronological order (earliest first): Brain, Creeper, Elk Cloner, Morris worm.
opts: Brain → Creeper → Elk Cloner → Morris worm
Creeper → Brain → Elk Cloner → Morris worm
Creeper → Elk Cloner → Brain → Morris worm
More than one of the above
exp: Creeper (1971) → Elk Cloner (1982) → Brain (1986) → Morris worm (1988).
concept: Creeper (1971) was an experimental self-copying program on ARPANET that displayed 'I'm the creeper, catch me if you can!'. Elk Cloner (1982) spread on Apple II floppy disks. Brain (1986), written by two brothers in Lahore, Pakistan, was the first virus for IBM PC (MS-DOS) computers. The Morris worm (1988) was one of the first worms to spread widely over the Internet.
why: A — Wrong. Brain (1986) came after Creeper (1971) and Elk Cloner (1982).
B — Wrong. Brain (1986) came after Elk Cloner (1982).
C — Correct. The years are 1971 → 1982 → 1986 → 1988.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work: Years: Creeper 1971, Elk Cloner 1982, Brain 1986, Morris worm 1988. Sorting by year gives Creeper → Elk Cloner → Brain → Morris worm.

q: Consider the following statements: I. A CAPTCHA is used to tell human users apart from automated programs (bots). II. A digital signature helps to verify who sent a message and that it was not changed. III. A firewall filters incoming and outgoing network traffic using a set of rules. Which of these is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three statements are true.
concept: CAPTCHA = Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart. A digital signature uses public-key cryptography to provide authentication, integrity and non-repudiation. A firewall (hardware or software) allows or blocks traffic according to rules, protecting a network from unauthorised access.
why: A — Correct. All three statements are true.
B — Wrong. III is also correct, so 'I and II only' is incomplete.
C — Wrong. I is also correct, so 'II and III only' is incomplete.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Converting readable data (plaintext) into a coded form (ciphertext) so that only authorised people can read it is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: This process is encryption, which is not among A–C.
concept: Encryption uses an algorithm and a key to turn plaintext into ciphertext; decryption uses a key to turn it back. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key (for example AES); asymmetric encryption uses a public key and a private key (for example RSA). HTTPS encrypts web traffic.
why: A — Wrong. Decryption is the reverse: turning ciphertext back into plaintext.
B — Wrong. Compression makes data smaller (for example ZIP); it is not meant to hide the data.
C — Wrong. Formatting prepares a disk for use (or sets the layout of text); it does not encode data.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The answer, encryption, is not listed.

q: Which of the following is NOT an image file format?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: GIF, PNG and TIFF are all image formats, so none of A–C fits the stem.
concept: Common image formats are JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF, SVG and WebP. GIF (Graphics Interchange Format) supports up to 256 colours and simple animation, but it is still an image format. Video formats include MP4, AVI, MKV and MOV.
why: A — Wrong. GIF is an image format (it can hold simple animations), so it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. PNG (Portable Network Graphics) is a lossless image format.
C — Wrong. TIFF (Tagged Image File Format) is an image format used in printing and scanning.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. All three are image formats, so none of them is the answer.
tip: Common mistake: the notes list GIF under video formats and VLC as a format. GIF is an image format; VLC is a media-player program, not a file format.

q: Which of the following is NOT a lossy compression format?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: PNG uses lossless compression; JPEG and MP3 are lossy.
concept: Lossy compression throws away some data that people hardly notice, which gives much smaller files: JPEG (photos), MP3 and AAC (audio), MP4/H.264 (video). Lossless compression keeps every bit, so the original can be rebuilt exactly: PNG, FLAC, ZIP.
why: A — Correct. PNG is lossless, so it is not a lossy format.
B — Wrong. JPEG is lossy (it discards fine detail), so it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. MP3 is lossy (it removes sounds people hardly hear), so it does not fit the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is NOT an audio file format?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: TIFF is an image format; AAC and FLAC are audio formats.
concept: Audio formats include MP3, AAC, WAV, FLAC, WMA, M4A and AIFF. FLAC is lossless, MP3 and AAC are lossy, and WAV is usually uncompressed. TIFF (Tagged Image File Format) is an image format.
why: A — Wrong. AAC (Advanced Audio Coding) is an audio format, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. FLAC (Free Lossless Audio Codec) is a lossless audio format.
C — Correct. TIFF is an image format, not an audio format.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following full forms are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three full forms are correct.
concept: Many format names come from the groups that made them: JPEG for photos and MPEG for video and audio (MP3 = MPEG-1 Audio Layer III; MP4 = MPEG-4 Part 14). PDF, created by Adobe in 1993, keeps a document looking the same on every device. Other full forms: GIF = Graphics Interchange Format, PNG = Portable Network Graphics.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. JPEG stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. MPEG stands for Moving Picture Experts Group.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. PDF stands for Portable Document Format.
D — Correct. All three full forms are correct.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following is a vector graphics format?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: BMP, JPEG and PNG are all raster (bitmap) formats; a vector format such as SVG is not listed.
concept: Raster (bitmap) images store a grid of pixels and become blocky when enlarged: BMP, JPEG, PNG, GIF. Vector images store shapes as mathematical lines and curves, so they can be scaled without losing quality: SVG, EPS, AI. Logos and fonts are usually vector.
why: A — Wrong. BMP (bitmap) is a raster format.
B — Wrong. JPEG is a raster format for photographs.
C — Wrong. PNG is a raster format that stores a grid of pixels.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. A vector format such as SVG or EPS is not listed.
tip: Raster = pixels (BMP, JPEG, PNG, GIF); vector = shapes (SVG, EPS, AI).

q: Which of the following is a technique that marks the beginning of computer communications?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Time sharing let many users at terminals, often far away and linked by telephone lines, use one central computer at the same time; this linking of terminals and computers is taken as the beginning of computer communications.
concept: In the batch era (1950s), users handed in jobs on punched cards and there was no communication between the user and the computer while jobs ran. Time-sharing systems of the 1960s, such as CTSS at MIT (1961), let many users work interactively through terminals, and remote terminals were connected to the computer over communication lines. This is why data-communication books treat time sharing as the start of computer communications, which later led to networks such as ARPANET.
why: A — Wrong. 'User environment' only means the setting or interface in which a user works; it is not a communication technique.
B — Wrong. In a batch environment jobs were collected and run one after another with no user interaction and no terminal communication.
C — Correct. Time sharing connected many terminals to one computer and is taken as the start of computer communications.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Honest note: the wording comes from an old MCQ bank and is vague ('user environment' and 'batch environment' are not communication techniques at all). The expected key is clear: Time Sharing, which is also the key that exam-solution sites give for this TRE question. The examiner most likely intended C.

q: Which language is better for writing structured code?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Pascal was designed by Niklaus Wirth (1970) to teach and encourage structured programming.
concept: Structured programming builds programs from three control structures (sequence, selection and repetition) and avoids GOTO jumps. Pascal was created with blocks (begin … end), procedures and strong data types for exactly this purpose. Early FORTRAN and BASIC relied heavily on GOTO and line numbers; later versions (FORTRAN 77/90, QBasic) added structured features, but Pascal is the classic answer.
why: A — Correct. Pascal was designed for structured programming and was widely used to teach it.
B — Wrong. Early FORTRAN (1957) was made for scientific calculation and relied on GOTO statements; it was not designed around structured programming.
C — Wrong. Classic BASIC (1964) used line numbers and GOTO and was designed for beginners, not for structured code.
D — Wrong. Only A is the language designed for structured programming.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Later versions of FORTRAN and BASIC do support structured code, so 'better' must be read historically; Pascal is the language that was designed for it.

q: Which language does a browser use to display information from the World Wide Web?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Web pages are written in HTML (HyperText Markup Language), styled with CSS and made interactive with JavaScript. HTML is not among A–C, so the answer is E.
concept: A browser downloads HTML files from web servers and renders (displays) them. HTML describes the structure of the page (headings, paragraphs, links, images); CSS gives the look and JavaScript adds behaviour. Tim Berners-Lee created HTML together with HTTP and the first browser (1990).
why: A — Wrong. Every program finally runs as machine code on the CPU, but web pages are not written or sent in machine code; the browser displays pages written in HTML.
B — Wrong. Assembly language is a low-level language for programming close to the hardware; it is not used for web pages.
C — Wrong. Some browsers are themselves written in C++, but the information they display from the web is written in HTML, not C++.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The expected answer is HTML, which is not listed.
tip: Honest note: the wording is loose. Someone could argue that a browser 'uses' C++ (engines such as Chrome's are written in it) or machine code (all programs run as machine code). But the question asks about the language of the information displayed from the WWW, which is HTML. The examiner most likely intended E.

q: Select the true statement for compiler.
opts: The input of the compiler is source program.
It translates the source code into object code as a whole.
The output of the compiler is object code.
More than one of the above
exp: All three statements are the standard textbook description of a compiler (source program in, whole program translated at once, object code out), so more than one option is true.
concept: A compiler takes the source program (in a high-level language) as input, translates the whole program at once, and produces an object program (object code) as output. The linker then turns object code into an executable file. An interpreter, by contrast, translates and runs one statement at a time and produces no object file.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The source program written by the programmer is the compiler's input.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A compiler translates the complete program in one go, unlike an interpreter.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The compiler's output is the object program (object code).
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one option is correct.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Some compilers produce assembly code or an executable directly, but in standard textbooks the compiler's output is object code. When all three options of a 'select the true statement' question are true, the answer is D.

q: Who is the father of computer?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Charles Babbage, who designed the Difference Engine and the Analytical Engine, is called the father of the computer.
concept: Charles Babbage (1791–1871) designed the Difference Engine (1822) and the Analytical Engine (1837). The Analytical Engine had a 'mill' (like a CPU) and a 'store' (like memory) and took input on punched cards, the main parts of a modern computer, so Babbage is called the father of the computer. Ada Lovelace wrote programs for it and is called the first programmer.
why: A — Wrong. James Gosling created Java (1995) and is called the father of Java.
B — Correct. Charles Babbage is the father of the computer.
C — Wrong. Dennis Ritchie created the C language (1972) and co-created Unix.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: Which of the following natural elements is the primary element in computer chips?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Computer chips are built on wafers of silicon, a semiconductor.
concept: Silicon is a semiconductor: its conductivity can be controlled by adding tiny amounts of other elements (doping). It is plentiful (sand is mostly silicon dioxide), forms a good insulating oxide layer and can be grown into very pure crystals. Transistors, ICs and microprocessors are built on silicon wafers, which gave Silicon Valley its name.
why: A — Wrong. Ordinary computer chips are not made from carbon; carbon materials such as graphene are still being researched for future chips.
B — Correct. Silicon is the main element of computer chips.
C — Wrong. Iron is a metal conductor, not a semiconductor, so chips are not built on it.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The brain of any computer system is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The CPU is called the brain of the computer because it processes all instructions and controls the other parts.
concept: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is called the brain of the computer because it fetches, decodes and executes instructions and controls all other parts. It contains the ALU (calculations and comparisons), the Control Unit (directs operations) and registers (fast temporary storage).
why: A — Wrong. The ALU is only one part of the CPU; it does the arithmetic and logic.
B — Wrong. Memory stores data and programs but does not process them or control the computer.
C — Correct. The CPU is the brain of the computer.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Some books call the Control Unit the 'brain of the CPU'; for the whole computer system the answer is the CPU.

q: When a key is pressed on keyboard, which standard is used for converting the keystroke into the corresponding bits?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Characters typed on a PC keyboard are represented by ASCII codes (for example 'A' = 65 = 1000001 in binary), so ASCII is the expected answer.
concept: ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange, 1963) is a 7-bit code for 128 characters: letters, digits, punctuation and control codes. PCs store typed characters as ASCII or Unicode, whose first 128 codes are the same as ASCII. NCERT Class 11 Computer Science (Chapter 2) uses this very example: pressing the key 'A' gives the code 65, which is its ASCII value. EBCDIC is an 8-bit code used mainly on IBM mainframes. ANSI (American National Standards Institute) is a standards organisation, not a character code itself.
why: A — Wrong. ANSI is the American National Standards Institute, an organisation that publishes standards; ASCII was developed under its predecessor body, but the character code itself is ASCII.
B — Correct. ASCII gives each typed character its binary code.
C — Wrong. EBCDIC (Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code) is used mainly on IBM mainframes, not for ordinary keyboard input on PCs.
D — Wrong. Only ASCII is the standard used for PC keystrokes, so 'More than one' does not apply.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Honest note: the wording is loose. Strictly, the keyboard first sends a scan code, which the computer then maps to a character code. A few online answer pages key ANSI, because 'ANSI' is also used loosely for Windows code pages, but ANSI is a standards body, not a character code. Most solution sites key ASCII for this question (it also appeared in the IB ACIO 2013 paper), and NCERT supports it.The examiner most likely intended B (ASCII).

q: What difference do the fifth generation computers have from other generation computers?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Each generation is defined by its technology, and the fifth generation is marked by new technology such as ULSI chips, parallel processing and artificial intelligence; so 'technological advancement' is the intended answer.
concept: Computer generations are separated by their main technology: vacuum tubes (1st), transistors (2nd), ICs (3rd), VLSI microprocessors (4th), and ULSI, parallel processing and AI (5th). Fifth-generation computers aim to understand natural language, learn and reason. Programming styles such as OOP do not define a generation.
why: A — Correct. The fifth generation differs by its technology: ULSI, parallel processing and AI.
B — Wrong. Object-oriented programming is a programming style (Simula 1967, Smalltalk, C++) used on fourth-generation machines too; it does not define the fifth generation.
C — Wrong. 'Scientific code' is not a feature of any generation; scientific programs have been written since the earliest computers (for example in FORTRAN).
D — Wrong. Only A fits, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Honest note: the question is vague, because every generation was a technological advance over the one before. It comes from an old online question bank (the same options plus 'All of the above'), and the widely accepted answer is 'Technological advancement', the only option that names what separates the generations. Neither object-oriented programming nor 'scientific code' defines the fifth generation (the Japanese fifth-generation project was built on logic programming and AI). The examiner most likely intended A.

q: Source code is available to view, modify and redistribute in
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Open-source software publishes its source code, and its licence lets anyone view, modify and redistribute it.
concept: Open-source software makes its source code public, and its licence (GPL, MIT, Apache, BSD) gives everyone the right to view, change and share it. Proprietary software keeps its source code secret. Note that open-source software is itself licensed; in this question 'licensed' means commercially licensed software, where you buy only the right to use it.
why: A — Correct. Open source allows viewing, modifying and redistributing the source code.
B — Wrong. A licence alone does not give access to source code; most commercially licensed software (such as MS Office) is closed source. Here 'licensed' means paid, closed software.
C — Wrong. Proprietary software keeps its source code secret and does not allow modification or redistribution.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Do not conclude that open source has no licence. It does; the licence is what grants the freedoms.

q: Machine language is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three are standard properties of machine language, so more than one option is true and the answer is D.
concept: Machine language is written in binary (0s and 1s) and is run directly by the CPU, so it is the fastest and needs no translator. But each CPU family has its own instruction set, so it is machine dependent. Writing long strings of 0s and 1s and remembering numeric opcodes and addresses makes it difficult to program and error prone, and also hard to debug and modify.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A program written for one CPU family's instruction set will not run on another.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Programmers must remember binary opcodes and memory addresses.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Long strings of 0s and 1s make mistakes easy to make and hard to find.
D — Correct. All three statements are true.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: The classic version of this question has the option 'All of the above'; in the TRE format the equivalent is D.

q: An assembly language is a/an
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Assembly language is a low-level (second-generation) language whose mnemonics map almost one-to-one to machine instructions.
concept: Assembly language (2GL) uses mnemonics such as MOV and ADD; each instruction maps almost one-to-one to a machine instruction, so it is low-level and machine dependent. An assembler translates it into machine code. 'Middle-level' is a label sometimes given to C, because C has high-level features plus low-level access to memory.
why: A — Correct. Assembly language is a low-level language.
B — Wrong. 'Middle-level' is a label used for C, not for assembly language.
C — Wrong. Assembly language has nothing to do with the Internet; web languages include HTML, JavaScript and PHP.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct, so 'More than one of the above' does not apply.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A compiler is a translating program which
opts: translates instruction of a high-level language into machine language
translates entire source program into machine language program
It is not involved in program's execution
More than one of the above
exp: All three describe a compiler in the usual textbook way: it translates high-level code into machine language, does it for the whole program at once, and is not needed while the translated program runs; so the answer is D.
concept: A compiler converts a high-level source program into a machine-language (object) program in one go. After compilation, the object/executable program runs on its own; the compiler plays no part during execution. An interpreter, in contrast, is active during execution because it translates and runs each statement in turn.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A compiler's job is to translate high-level language instructions into machine language.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. It translates the entire source program at once, unlike an interpreter.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Once translation is done, the compiled program runs without the compiler.
D — Correct. All three statements are true.
E — Wrong. More than one of A–C is true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Honest note: option C is loosely worded, but it means the compiler is not needed while the compiled program runs, which is true. The classic source of this question keys 'All of the above', which is D in the TRE format.
